course.title: Backend Development and API Design
course.description: Understand HTTP well enough to design an API that clients can rely on: methods, status codes, caching, resources, JSON, contracts, pagination, errors, security and the structure of a service behind it.
course.audience: Someone who can write short Python functions and has seen a database query, and who now wants to build or consume web services. No web framework knowledge is needed; the course is about the protocol and the design decisions, not about any one framework.

paragraphs: A request to a web service is a few lines of text. The first line names a method and an address, such as POST /orders, and the answer begins with a status code, such as 201 for an order that now exists, followed by header fields and a body. An API built on HTTP is a set of agreements about what those lines mean: which requests only read and which change something, which status code reports which outcome, and what shape the data in the body takes.

Other programs rely on those agreements and cannot ask what you meant by them. A client whose request times out can repeat it safely only if the method promised that a repeat leaves the server as one copy would, a cache can reuse a stored response only if the headers say how long it stays fresh, and renaming one field in a response breaks every program that reads it. Backend development is the work of keeping those promises with real callers, some of whom make mistakes and some of whom are hostile.

Most of the questions this raises can be settled by following what one particular request would do, and some can be settled by arithmetic: how long a cached copy stays fresh, how many pages a collection of 137 items takes at 25 to a page, how long a client waits before its fifth retry. With that habit you can read a raw request and say what it asks for, judge whether an API's methods and status codes mean what they say, and find the places where a caller could read another person's data or make the server do something it should not.
outcomes: You'll be able to read and write a raw HTTP request and response.
You'll be able to choose methods and status codes that do what they promise, and decide what is safe to retry.
You'll be able to work out cache freshness and use conditional requests.
You'll be able to design resources, URLs and JSON bodies, and describe them in OpenAPI.
You'll be able to paginate a collection correctly, shape errors, and make a POST safe to retry.
You'll be able to tell authentication from authorisation, and spot injection, mass assignment and missing object-level checks.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on How Computers Solve Problems, Python for Data Analysis, SQL: From Rows to Reports, How Computers and Networks Work.

modules.title: Speaking HTTP
modules.description: What a request and response contain, what the methods and status codes promise, and how caching saves work.

modules.title: Designing the interface
modules.description: Resources and URLs, JSON bodies, a written contract in OpenAPI, and the habits that make an API easy to live with: pagination, clear errors, safe retries and careful change.

modules.title: Trust and load
modules.description: Who is calling, what they may do, what input to distrust, and how to behave when traffic is heavy.

modules.title: Structuring a service
modules.description: Layers, transactions and background work, tied together with the earlier ideas.

concepts.title: Request
concepts.summary: An HTTP request is a request line (method, target, version), header fields, a blank line and an optional body.

concepts.title: Response
concepts.summary: A response is a status line (version, status code, reason), header fields, a blank line and an optional body.

concepts.title: Header field
concepts.summary: A header field is a name and value that describes the message, such as Content-Type for the body's media type and Content-Length for its size in bytes.

concepts.title: Safe method
concepts.summary: A method is safe when its defined semantics are read-only, as for GET and HEAD, so a client may issue it without asking.

concepts.title: Idempotent method
concepts.summary: A method is idempotent when sending the same request several times has the same intended effect on the server as sending it once, as for PUT and DELETE.

concepts.title: Retry rule
concepts.summary: Because a lost response is indistinguishable from a lost request, only safe and idempotent requests may be repeated automatically.

concepts.title: Status class
concepts.summary: The first digit gives the class: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

concepts.title: 401 and 403
concepts.summary: 401 means the request lacks valid credentials, 403 means the caller is identified but not allowed.

concepts.title: 400, 409 and 422
concepts.summary: 400 means the request could not be understood, 409 means it is valid but conflicts with the current state, and 422 means it was understood but its content cannot be processed.

concepts.title: Freshness
concepts.summary: A cached response is fresh while its age is less than its freshness lifetime, such as Cache-Control: max-age=300, and can be reused without contacting the server.

concepts.title: Validator
concepts.summary: An ETag or Last-Modified value identifies a version of a resource so a client can ask whether it has changed.

concepts.title: Revalidation
concepts.summary: A stale response is revalidated with If-None-Match, and a 304 Not Modified reply with no body lets the cache reuse its copy.

concepts.title: Resource
concepts.summary: A resource is a thing the API exposes, named by a URL, and the methods act on it.

concepts.title: URL parts
concepts.summary: A URL has a scheme, host, path, query and fragment; the path names the resource and the query narrows or shapes the result.

concepts.title: Path template
concepts.summary: A template such as /orders/{id} describes a family of paths, and a router extracts the named parts.

concepts.title: Representation
concepts.summary: A representation is a particular encoding of a resource's state, chosen by the client with Accept and declared by the server with Content-Type.

concepts.title: JSON syntax
concepts.summary: JSON has objects, arrays, strings, numbers, true, false and null; it forbids comments, trailing commas, single quotes and leading zeros.

concepts.title: Number care
concepts.summary: JSON numbers have no fixed precision, but most parsers read them as 64-bit floats, so binary fractions and integers above 2^53 lose exactness.

concepts.title: OpenAPI document
concepts.summary: An OpenAPI document is a machine-readable description of an HTTP API: its paths, operations, parameters, request bodies, responses and schemas.

concepts.title: Schema
concepts.summary: A schema describes the allowed shape of a JSON value, including property types and which properties are required.

concepts.title: Contract
concepts.summary: The description is a contract that clients, servers, tests and documentation can all be generated or checked against.

concepts.title: Offset paging
concepts.summary: Offset paging asks for the items after skipping offset rows, which is easy but shifts whenever rows are inserted or deleted earlier in the list.

concepts.title: Keyset paging
concepts.summary: Keyset paging asks for items after the last one seen, using the sort key, so earlier changes do not shift later pages.

concepts.title: Cursor
concepts.summary: A cursor is an opaque token that encodes where to resume, so clients do not depend on its content.

concepts.title: Problem details
concepts.summary: RFC 9457 defines a JSON error body served as application/problem+json with type, title, status, detail and instance members.

concepts.title: Idempotency key
concepts.summary: The client sends a unique key with a request, and the server stores the result under that key so a repeat returns the stored result instead of acting again.

concepts.title: Effect once
concepts.summary: Retries can deliver a request many times, so safety comes from the server recognising repeats, not from hoping the network delivers once.

concepts.title: Breaking change
concepts.summary: A change is breaking if a client written against the old contract can fail: removing or renaming a field, changing its type, or newly requiring a request field.

concepts.title: Tolerant reader
concepts.summary: Clients that ignore unknown fields let servers add fields without breaking them.

concepts.title: Deprecation and sunset
concepts.summary: A deprecation warns that something will go, with a date, and the Deprecation and Sunset headers announce this in responses.

concepts.title: Authentication
concepts.summary: Authentication establishes who is calling, by a password, a key, a token or a certificate.

concepts.title: Signed token
concepts.summary: A signed token carries claims plus a keyed hash (HMAC) so the server can verify, without a lookup, that it issued them; the claims are readable by anyone.

concepts.title: Password hashing
concepts.summary: Passwords are stored as slow, salted hashes (Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2) so a stolen table is expensive to guess against.

concepts.title: Object-level authorisation
concepts.summary: Every request for a specific object must check that the caller may access that object, not only that the caller is logged in.

concepts.title: Injection
concepts.summary: Building a query by concatenating input lets input change the query's structure; parameterised queries keep data and code apart.

concepts.title: Mass assignment
concepts.summary: Copying every field of a request body onto a stored object lets a caller set fields they should not, so accept only an allowlist.

concepts.title: Token bucket
concepts.summary: A token bucket holds up to a capacity of tokens, refills at a fixed rate, and spends one per request, which allows bursts up to the capacity and a steady rate over time.

concepts.title: 429 and Retry-After
concepts.summary: A server over the limit replies 429 Too Many Requests and may add Retry-After to say when to try again.

concepts.title: Exponential backoff with jitter
concepts.summary: A client that retries waits longer after each failure, for example base x 2^attempt up to a cap, with random jitter so many clients do not retry together.

concepts.title: Layers
concepts.summary: A handler translates HTTP to and from calls, a service applies business rules, and a repository talks to storage, so each can change and be tested alone.

concepts.title: Transaction boundary
concepts.summary: One request that changes several rows should do so inside one database transaction, opened and committed by the service layer.

concepts.title: At-least-once delivery
concepts.summary: A queue that retries until acknowledged delivers some messages more than once, so consumers must tolerate duplicates.

lessons.title: Anatomy of an HTTP exchange

steps.headline: A message is lines of text

lead.text: Read the request in the opening figure from the top. Its first line, `POST /orders HTTP/1.1`, is the **request line**, and it holds three things separated by single spaces: a *method*, which says what the client wants done, a *target*, which says what it wants it done to, and the version of the protocol being spoken.

Each line below it has the form name, colon, value, and is called a **header field**: a piece of information about the message rather than part of its content. A line with nothing on it ends the headers, and whatever follows is the **body**, the content the message carries. A request to read something usually has no body, while a request to create something carries the thing to be created. The response has the same layout with a **status line** in place of the request line, and its first line states whether the request succeeded.

reveal.text: The next screen shows what the browser keeps for itself and what it sends.

lead.text: The scheme, `https`, tells the browser how to connect, and the host, `shop.example`, tells it where; the browser then sends the **path**, `/search`, and the **query**, the text after the question mark, as the target. The query is a list of `name=value` pairs joined by ampersands, so `q=rust` and `page=2` are two pairs.

The host still has to reach the server, because one machine often serves many sites, and it travels in the `Host` header instead. The **fragment**, `#reviews`, is different again: it tells the browser which part of the page to scroll to, so it is *never sent*.

diagram.alt: The address https://shop.example/search?q=rust&page=2#reviews split into scheme, host, path, query and fragment, and then the request line the server receives, which holds only the path and query.
diagram.caption: Only the path and the query reach the request line. Use the buttons to compare the address with what is sent.

reveal.text: A name that repeats, such as tag, is how a client sends several values for one parameter.

lead.text: **Host** names the site being asked. **Content-Type** gives the **media type** of the body, a label such as `application/json` that tells the receiver how to read the bytes. **Content-Length** gives the size of the body in bytes, so that the receiver knows where the message ends. **Accept** is the client's list of media types it can use in the reply, and **Authorization** carries credentials.

The split between the fields matters when you read a message: `Content-Type` and `Content-Length` describe the body that is *in* this message, while `Accept` describes the reply the sender hopes to *get*.

reveal.text: A server that receives JSON without this field has to guess, and many refuse to.

lead.text: The body `{"item":"pen","qty":3}` has 22 characters, and each is plain ASCII, so it is also 22 bytes and the request carries `Content-Length: 22`. Text is sent as bytes, though, and JSON is normally encoded in UTF-8, which uses one byte for ASCII characters and more for others: the letter é takes two bytes, and ü does too.

The header counts the *bytes*, since that is what the receiver reads from the connection. A body with one accented letter therefore has a `Content-Length` one greater than its character count, and a receiver told 30 when 31 bytes follow will cut the body short, and one told 31 when only 30 follow will wait for a byte that never arrives.

steps.headline: Find the Content-Length for the body {"city":"Zürich"}.

workedSteps.text: Count the characters, including the braces, the quotation marks and the colon.
Find the characters that are not ASCII. Only ü is, and it needs two bytes, not one.
Each extra byte raises the total, so add one for the ü.
The header is Content-Length: 18.

steps.headline: Find the Content-Length for the body {"name":"Zoë","qty":2}.

workedSteps.text: Count the characters: the body has 22.
Find the characters that are not ASCII. Only ë is.
In UTF-8 the ë takes two bytes, where each ASCII character takes one.

lead.text: Before any message is sent, the client has to find the server. It looks the host name up in DNS to get an address, opens a connection to that address, and then writes its request on the connection, as the figure steps through. The server reads the request, decides what to do with it, and writes a response on the same connection.

The response has a status line with the version, a three-digit **status code** such as 201, and a short reason such as Created. Responses use some of the same fields: `Content-Type` and `Content-Length` describe the body, and a field of their own, **Location**, gives the address of something the server has just made.

diagram.caption: The client speaks first and the server answers. Use the buttons to step through the exchange.

lessons.orientation: Read and write a raw HTTP/1.1 request and response, and state what each part is for.
lessons.nextAction: Say which methods are safe and idempotent, and predict what happens when a request is delivered twice.

blocks.text: A browser that asks a shop to create an order sends text that begins `POST /orders HTTP/1.1`, continues with lines such as `Content-Type: application/json`, and ends with the order itself, `{"item":"pen","qty":3}`. The server replies with text of the same layout, starting `HTTP/1.1 201 Created` and ending with a body of its own, `{"id":812,"status":"new"}`. An **HTTP exchange** is that pair of messages, one request and the response to it.
Both messages have the same parts in the same order, a first line, header fields, a blank line and a body, so a server can read one line by line and know at each point what it is looking at.

diagram.caption: Both messages have the same four parts in the same order. Use the buttons to switch between the request and the response.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read a raw HTTP request and response, split a request line into its parts, and work out the Content-Length of a body.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later idea in the course is a rule about some part of these two messages.

recap.keyIdea: An HTTP request and response are each a first line, header fields, a blank line and an optional body, and the headers describe the message while the body carries the data.

blocks.text: You read a request line as method, target and version, and found that the target holds only the path and the query: the host goes in the Host header, and the fragment is never sent. You also saw that Content-Length counts bytes, so a body with an accented letter has a length greater than its character count.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the first word of the request line, the method, and at what it promises about repeating a request.

lessons.title: Methods, safety and idempotence

reveal.text: The result depends on what kind of request it was, and the next screens set out why.

lead.text: The server has either never seen the request or seen it and failed to answer, and nothing on the client's side separates the two. Whether to send the request again is therefore a decision about what *another* delivery would do, and HTTP lets the method named in the [[request line|The first line of a request: method, target and version. Met in "Anatomy of an HTTP exchange".]] answer that in advance.

A method is **safe** when its defined meaning is read-only, so a client may send it without asking anyone. A method is **idempotent** when sending the same request several times has the same intended effect on the server as sending it once. Every safe method is idempotent, but an idempotent method need not be safe: a `PUT` that sets a product's price to 40 changes the server, and yet sending it twice leaves the price at 40, exactly as once does.

afterFigure.text: GET and HEAD, which fetch a resource and its headers, are both safe and idempotent. PUT, which replaces a resource at a known address, and DELETE, which removes one, are idempotent but not safe. POST and PATCH are neither, because a POST has the meaning the server chooses to give it, and PATCH applies a change that may depend on the current state.

reveal.text: A request that names its end state can be delivered again without moving the counter further.

lead.text: Take `DELETE /orders/7`. The first delivery removes the order and the server answers 204, which means it succeeded and has nothing to send back; the second finds no order 7 and answers 404, which means there is nothing at that address. The responses differ, and yet after one delivery and after two the shop holds exactly the same orders, so `DELETE` is idempotent. The numbers are the subject of the next lesson, and for now it is enough that a response may change.

It follows that idempotence promises something about the *intended effect on the server*, and says nothing about what the client reads back. A client that treats a 404 on a retried `DELETE` as a failure has misread the promise, since the order it wanted removed is indeed gone.

reveal.text: Only the first delivery changes the state, which is the definition of idempotence at work.

lead.text: Combining the two ideas gives the **retry rule**: a client library may resend a `GET`, a `HEAD`, a `PUT` or a `DELETE` after a failure without asking anyone, because the worst outcome is that the server does what it already did. A `POST` or a `PATCH` must not be resent on its own account, since the first copy may have been carried out.

The same reliance on safety explains why GET must never change data. Browsers prefetch links, caches answer from a stored copy without troubling the server, and search crawlers follow every link on a page, and all of them assume that a GET changes nothing. A page that deletes an item when its link is fetched with GET has handed the deletion to every one of these programs.

steps.headline: Decide whether a client may resend PUT /counter with {"value": 15} after a lost response.

workedSteps.text: The client cannot know whether the first copy arrived, so consider both cases.
If the first copy arrived, the counter already holds 15 when the resend arrives.
If the first copy never arrived, the resend sets the counter from 10 to 15 for the first time.
Both cases end at 15, so the resend is safe to send automatically.

steps.headline: Decide whether a client may resend POST /counter/add with {"n": 3} after a lost response.

workedSteps.text: Again there are two cases. If the first copy never arrived, the resend adds 3 once and the counter ends at 13.
If the first copy did arrive, the resend is a second request to add 3.
The two cases end in different states, so this resend must not be automatic.

reveal.text: A GET that changes data should have been a DELETE, which software knows not to follow or resend carelessly.

lead.text: A common belief holds that `POST` creates things and `PUT` updates them, and the retry rule above shows why that belief is worth correcting. **PUT** carries a complete new version of the resource and sends it to the address where that resource lives, so using it to create something is quite normal when the client chooses the address, and using it again simply replaces what is there. **POST** hands the server a request to process in whatever way its design says, such as adding an order to a collection, and the server chooses the address.

The choice between them is therefore a choice about the retry rule. If the client names the final state and the address, PUT's guarantee applies. If the server has to do something with the request, POST's lack of a guarantee applies, and the client has to be careful about sending it twice.

reveal.text: Because the method states the end state, it keeps the same guarantee on every delivery.

lessons.orientation: Say which HTTP methods are safe and idempotent, and predict the effect of a request delivered twice.
lessons.nextAction: Read a status code and choose the one that says what happened.

blocks.text: The first word of a request line, such as GET, PUT, POST or DELETE, tells every program that handles the request what it may do with it. A client library whose request has timed out will send a GET or a PUT again without asking anyone, yet it will not send a POST again on its own, because with no reply it cannot know whether the server received the first copy and acted on it or never saw it at all.

The difference lies in what a second delivery would do. A method is **idempotent** when delivering the same request several times leaves the server as one delivery would, and `GET` and `PUT` have that property while `POST` does not.

intro.whyItMatters: Whether a failed request may be repeated is decided by its method.

recap.keyIdea: A safe method only reads and an idempotent method leaves the same state when repeated, so only safe and idempotent requests may be resent automatically.

blocks.text: You compared a PUT that sets a counter to 15 with a POST that adds 5, and found that a second delivery changes the outcome of the POST alone. DELETE showed that idempotence concerns the state the server ends in, since a second delete may answer 404 and leave the shop exactly as the first did.

lessons.title: Status codes that say what happened

reveal.text: The next screen sorts the codes into the classes that tell the software around the client what to do.

lead.text: A response begins with a three-digit **status code**, and the first digit gives its **class**. A 2xx code reports success, a 3xx code sends the client elsewhere, a 4xx code says the *request* was at fault, and a 5xx code says the *server* was. Programs act on that digit before any person reads the body, so a class is a statement about who has to change something: nobody for 2xx, the client for 4xx, and the server for 5xx.

Three success codes cover most of what an API returns. **200 OK** reports that the request worked and has a body describing the result. **201 Created** reports that a resource was made, and is sent with a `Location` header giving its address. **204 No Content** reports that the request worked and that there is no body, as after a `PUT` whose new version the client already holds.

reveal.text: The client then knows the order is gone and has no body to read.

lead.text: **400 Bad Request** says the request could not be understood, such as a body that is not valid JSON. **401 Unauthorized** says the request lacks valid credentials, despite the word in its name, so the caller has not been identified. **403 Forbidden** says the caller is identified and is not allowed. **404 Not Found** says nothing exists at that address.

**409 Conflict** says the request is well formed but clashes with the current state, as when a seat that another customer holds is booked again. **429 Too Many Requests** says the client is sending faster than allowed.

reveal.text: A 401 would send the client off to log in again, which could never help here.

steps.headline: Server errors and the order of checks

lead.text: A **5xx** code means the server failed on a request that may have been fine: **500 Internal Server Error** is the general code for an unexpected failure, and **503 Service Unavailable** means it cannot serve right now, for example when overloaded. The distinction matters for retrying, since a 5xx says that trying again later might succeed, whereas a 4xx says the same request will fail again until it is changed.

The 3xx codes redirect, and a later lesson covers 304, but one point belongs here: a client can only act correctly if the server chose the code deliberately. The server checks the request in a fixed order, and each check has its own exit, so a request that cannot be parsed leaves at the first, and one that is parsed but not permitted leaves at the third.

diagram.caption: A request leaves at the first check it fails, and the code on that exit is what the client receives. Use the buttons to follow a request that fails one check.

steps.headline: Follow PUT /invoices/9 from a caller with a valid token for user A, when invoice 9 belongs to user B.

workedSteps.text: The server first parses the request, and the JSON body is valid, so this check passes.
It then looks at the token, which is valid and names user A, so the caller is authenticated.
The third check asks whether A may change invoice 9. The invoice belongs to B, so the request leaves here.
The checks that follow, finding the resource and checking its state, are never reached.
The client receives 403 Forbidden.

steps.headline: Follow POST /orders/42/cancellation from the order's owner, with a valid token, when order 42 has already shipped.

workedSteps.text: The request parses, so the first check passes.
The caller is identified and owns order 42, so the next two checks pass as well.
Order 42 exists, so the fourth check passes, but it has already shipped.

lead.text: Three codes are easily confused, and the question to ask of each is where the fault lies. A body that is not valid JSON never reaches the application, so it is a **400**. A body that is valid JSON and whose fields are well formed, but which asks for something that clashes with what the server already holds, such as cancelling an order that has already shipped, is a **409**. A body that is understood and valid in form, but whose content cannot be processed, such as a date of birth in the future, is a **422 Unprocessable Content**.

The line between 400 and 422 is a matter of design, and many APIs use 400 for both. What matters is that each code is used for one kind of fault and that the API says which, so that a client can tell what to change without a person reading the body.

reveal.text: A client that sees this code knows the request itself need not change, only the data it names.
A 4xx or 5xx code lets this software act without ever opening the body.

blocks.text: Every HTTP response begins with a line such as `HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found` or `HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable`, and the three-digit **status code** in it is written to be read by software. The first digit sorts the outcome: 2 says the request worked, 4 says the request was at fault, and 5 says the server was.

intro.whyItMatters: Software acts on the status code before it reads the body.

recap.keyIdea: A status code says what happened, in a class that says who must change something, so the code has to be chosen to match the outcome.

blocks.text: The first digit sets the class: 2xx for success, 4xx for a fault in the request and 5xx for a fault in the server. Within 4xx, 401 means the caller is not identified, 403 means the caller is identified and refused, 400 means the request could not be read and 409 means it clashes with current state.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at a status that saves work, 304, and at the headers that let a stored copy be reused.

lessons.title: Caching and conditional requests

reveal.text: The next screen gives the rule for this, and shows what happens when the time runs out.

lead.text: **Cache-Control: max-age=300** gives the response a **freshness lifetime** of 300 seconds, counted from the moment it was generated. A cache that stores it measures the copy's **age**, the time since then, and while the age is *less than* the lifetime the copy is **fresh**, so the cache answers from its own store without contacting the origin, the server that holds the original.

A **shared cache**, such as a content delivery network placed between a thousand users and one server, answers all of them from a single stored copy, so the server's work and the bytes on the network are spent once instead of a thousand times.

reveal.text: Once the remaining time reaches zero, the copy is stale and the cache must do something else.

lead.text: When the age reaches the lifetime the copy is **stale**, which means it has to be checked before it is used again, and it does not mean it is wrong or has been removed. The origin gave the response an **ETag**, a short string that identifies this version of the resource, such as `"v7"`. The cache sends the request again with **If-None-Match: "v7"**, which says: send the body only if the version is no longer `v7`.

If the version is still `v7` the origin answers **304 Not Modified** with no body, and the cache keeps its copy and treats it as fresh again from that moment. If the resource has changed, the origin answers 200 with the new body and a new `ETag`. This is **revalidation**. A 304 is therefore a success: it costs a round trip, and it saves the whole body, which in the figure is 48,000 bytes. The older validator **Last-Modified**, a date, works the same way with `If-Modified-Since`.

diagram.alt: A cache sends a conditional GET with If-None-Match v7 to the origin. If the resource has changed the origin answers 200 with the new body of 48,000 bytes; if not it answers 304 Not Modified with no body.

reveal.text: The cache stores the new body and its new Last-Modified date, and the copy is fresh again from that moment.

lead.text: Two directives are often mixed up. **no-cache** does not mean *do not cache*: it lets a cache store the response, and requires it to revalidate before each reuse. **no-store** is the directive that forbids keeping the response at all, and it belongs on responses holding private data that should leave no copy behind. A third, **private**, allows only the user's own browser to store the response, and not a shared cache.

The lifetime itself is a choice about how often the data changes. A file whose name contains its version, such as `app.4f2a9c.js`, never changes under that name, so it can have a very long max-age. A response about the current user's account should be private and have a short lifetime, or none.

reveal.text: A directive that merely forces revalidation would still leave a copy behind.

steps.headline: Count the contacts with the origin for max-age=300 and requests at t = 0, 100, 200, 350, 400 and 500 seconds, for a resource that never changes.

workedSteps.text: At t = 0 the cache has nothing, so the request goes to the origin, and the copy is fresh until t = 300.
At t = 100 and t = 200 the copy is younger than 300 seconds, so the cache answers both itself.
At t = 350 the copy has been stored for a long time.
The age of 350 exceeds 300, so the cache revalidates, and a 304 makes the copy fresh until t = 650.
At t = 400 and t = 500 the copy is younger than 300 seconds again, so the cache answers both.
The origin was contacted at t = 0 and t = 350, which is 2 times for 6 requests.

steps.headline: Count the contacts for max-age=100 and requests at t = 0, 50, 120, 150 and 260 seconds, for a resource that never changes.

workedSteps.text: The request at t = 0 goes to the origin, and the copy is fresh until t = 100.
At t = 50 the copy is fresh. At t = 120 it is stale, so the cache revalidates and a 304 renews it until t = 220.
The copy was renewed at t = 120, so it stays fresh until t = 220. The requests at t = 150 and t = 260 are still to be checked against that.

reveal.text: Revalidation turns most of the traffic into headers, and the body travels only when there is something new.

lessons.orientation: Work out whether a cached response is still fresh, and explain how a validator avoids resending an unchanged body.
lessons.nextAction: Name the resources of an API and give them clear URLs.

blocks.text: A response can carry the header `Cache-Control: max-age=300`, which allows any program between the server and the reader to keep a copy and reuse it for the next 300 seconds without asking the server again. A **cache** is a program that does this, and the saving can be large: a product list of 48,000 bytes that a thousand people request in an hour would otherwise be built and sent a thousand times, which is 48,000,000 bytes of identical output, although the data may have changed only twice in that hour.
Once the 300 seconds have passed the copy is not thrown away, because the cache can ask the server whether it is still current, and if it is, the server answers with a short reply and no body.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to work out whether a cached response is still fresh, and explain how a validator lets a cache avoid resending an unchanged body.
intro.whyItMatters: Caching is the cheapest way to make an API faster, and its rules are simple arithmetic.

recap.keyIdea: A cached response is reused while its age is below its max-age, and once stale it is revalidated with its ETag, so an unchanged resource costs a 304 and not a new body.

blocks.text: You calculated freshness as the lifetime minus the age, counted the contacts with the origin for a series of requests, and saw that a 304 renews a stale copy without resending the body. no-cache stores and revalidates, whereas no-store forbids keeping the response.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from what the protocol does to what an API exposes, and asks how to choose the things that URLs name.

lessons.title: Resources and URLs

lead.text: A **resource** is a thing that an API exposes, such as an order or a customer, and a URL names it. The scheme and host say where to connect, and the **path**, `/v1/customers/17/orders`, names the resource, which here is the orders of customer 17. The **query**, `status=open&limit=20`, does not name anything new: it narrows or shapes what comes back, and the fragment, `#top`, is never sent.

The path is read in **segments**, the pieces between slashes. The first, `v1`, is a version, and the rest alternate between a collection, `customers`, and one member of it, 17, before moving on to a second collection, that customer's orders.

diagram.alt: The URL https://api.shop.example/v1/customers/17/orders?status=open&limit=20#top split into scheme, host, path, query and fragment, and then its path split into four segments: v1, customers, 17 and orders.
diagram.caption: The path names the resource, and the query narrows the result. Use the buttons to look at the parts and then at the path.

reveal.text: A router makes this count first, since a path can only match a template with the same number of segments.

lead.text: The paths `/orders` and `/orders/42` name two different resources. The first is a **collection**, the set of all orders, and the second is one **item** in it. As the opening figure shows, `GET /orders` lists the collection and `POST /orders` adds a new item to it, with the server choosing the item's address. `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` on `/orders/42` read, replace and remove that one order.

Because the method already carries the verb, the path should be a noun. A path such as `/getOrder` or `/deleteOrder` repeats what `GET` and `DELETE` say, and it forces every client to learn a vocabulary of verbs that HTTP already provides. A **collection** is usually a plural noun, and an item is the collection's path followed by its identifier.

reveal.text: The new address is returned in a Location header, as the first lesson showed.
The next screen shows what the unsafe design lets other software do.

lead.text: Not every operation is a create, a read or a delete, and cancelling an order is one example. The usual answer is to treat the action as a resource of its own: `POST /orders/42/cancellation` creates a cancellation of order 42, using a noun, and a method that is allowed to change state. The alternative `GET /orders/42/cancel` puts a verb in the path and changes data with a method that every crawler and prefetching browser assumes is safe, as the figure shows.

A path can also express a relationship. `/customers/17/orders` lists the orders of customer 17, and that reads clearly. Depth carries a cost, though, since every level of nesting makes the URL longer and ties the order to its parent.

diagram.alt: Two designs for cancelling order 42. A GET to /orders/42/cancel can be followed by a crawler and cancel the order. A POST to /orders/42/cancellation is never sent by a crawler.

lead.text: A server has to decide which code handles each request. It does so with **path templates** such as `/orders/{id}`, in which a segment in braces stands for any value, and a router tries a path against each template in turn. A path matches when it has the *same number of segments* as the template and every segment that is not in braces is equal. The segments in braces are captured: against `/orders/42`, the template `/orders/{id}` gives `id = 42`.

The figure shows both outcomes. `/orders/{id}/items/{item}` fits `/orders/42/items/7` and captures two values, but `/orders/{id}` does not fit `/orders/42/items`, since the path has one segment more. A router that finds no fit returns nothing, which in Python is `None`, and moves on to the next template.

blocks.text: The address `https://api.shop.example/v1/customers/17/orders?status=open&limit=20#top` is built from parts that do different jobs. The path, `/v1/customers/17/orders`, names a thing, here the orders of customer 17. A **resource** is a thing of this kind that an API exposes, such as an order or a customer, and its URL is its name.

The names an API gives its resources decide how easily it can be used, because a client that has seen `/orders` and `/orders/42` can guess that the first is the set of orders and the second is one of them, and the methods from the earlier lessons then supply the verbs without any new vocabulary.

recap.keyIdea: A URL path names a resource in nouns, the method says what to do to it, and a router matches a path to a template segment by segment.

blocks.text: You split a URL into its path, query and fragment and read the path in segments. A collection and its items get their own URLs, an action such as a cancellation becomes a noun under POST, and a path matches a template only when the counts of segments agree and the fixed segments are equal.

lessons.title: JSON and representations

reveal.text: The next screen sets out the rules of the grammar, and the figure shows three that catch people out.

lead.text: Order 42 is a resource, and nobody sends the resource itself over the network. What is sent is a **representation**, a particular encoding of its current state, and the same order can be encoded in more than one way. In the figure at the start of the lesson the client lists the media type it wants in an **Accept** header, and the server replies with that encoding and states which one it used in **Content-Type**.
Most APIs today offer one representation, **JSON**, short for JavaScript Object Notation. A server that cannot supply any of the listed types answers 406 Not Acceptable.

A JSON value is an **object** of named members in braces, an **array** of values in square brackets, a **string** in double quotes, a **number**, or one of the three words **true**, **false** and **null**. A parser either accepts a text as a whole or rejects it, because the grammar leaves no room for partial credit.

The rules that catch people are the ones where JSON is stricter than the language it came from. Strings and member names need double quotes, a comma may only separate two members, so a trailing comma is an error, a number cannot start with a zero, and there are no comments.

diagram.alt: Three pieces of text that look like JSON and are not: an object with a trailing comma, an object with single quotes, and a number with a leading zero. Each is shown with a short explanation of why it is rejected.
diagram.caption: JavaScript accepts all three, and JSON accepts none of them. Use the buttons to see each case.

cases.label: Trailing comma
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 250"><defs><marker id="mcomma" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="4" orient="auto"><path class="f-ink" d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z"/></marker></defs><text class="t-small t-muted" x="320" y="50" text-anchor="middle">The text</text><rect class="f-sunken s-ink w2" x="24" y="64" width="592" height="60" rx="8"/><text class="t-big" x="320" y="102" text-anchor="middle">{"a": 1,}</text><text class="t-bold t-error" x="320" y="170" text-anchor="middle">A comma must be followed by another member.</text><text class="t" x="320" y="204" text-anchor="middle">A trailing comma is allowed in JavaScript and forbidden in JSON.</text></svg>

cases.label: Single quotes
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 250"><defs><marker id="mquote" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="4" orient="auto"><path class="f-ink" d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z"/></marker></defs><text class="t-small t-muted" x="320" y="50" text-anchor="middle">The text</text><rect class="f-sunken s-ink w2" x="24" y="64" width="592" height="60" rx="8"/><text class="t-big" x="320" y="102" text-anchor="middle">{'a': 1}</text><text class="t-bold t-error" x="320" y="170" text-anchor="middle">Strings and names need double quotes.</text><text class="t" x="320" y="204" text-anchor="middle">JSON has no single-quoted strings.</text></svg>

cases.label: Leading zero
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 250"><defs><marker id="mzero" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="4" orient="auto"><path class="f-ink" d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z"/></marker></defs><text class="t-small t-muted" x="320" y="50" text-anchor="middle">The text</text><rect class="f-sunken s-ink w2" x="24" y="64" width="592" height="60" rx="8"/><text class="t-big" x="320" y="102" text-anchor="middle">{"a": 01}</text><text class="t-bold t-error" x="320" y="170" text-anchor="middle">A number may not start with a zero.</text><text class="t" x="320" y="204" text-anchor="middle">01 is rejected, while 0 and 0.1 are valid.</text></svg>

reveal.text: null is a value in its own right, and an API may rely on the difference between null and a field that is left out.

lead.text: A client is written against the shape of a body, so the shape has to stay put. Use the same name for the same thing everywhere, give a field one type in every response, send identifiers as strings so that they can change form later, and write timestamps in ISO 8601, such as 2026-11-03T09:30:00Z, which is unambiguous in any time zone.

Three states are easily confused. A field can be *absent*, *null* or the *empty string*, and they mean different things. In a `PATCH` that updates a profile, `{"nick": null}` clears the nickname, a body that leaves `nick` out leaves it as it was, and `{"nick": ""}` sets it to a string with no characters. A server that treats all three alike cannot support partial updates.

Most JSON parsers read a number into a 64-bit floating-point value, which holds a binary fraction. Many decimal fractions have no exact binary form, so 0.1 + 0.2 comes out as 0.30000000000000004, and 4.35 x 100 as 434.99999999999994. A total built from such values can miss by a tiny amount, and a payment that is wrong by a fraction of a cent is still wrong.

The remedy is to hold money as an integer number of the smallest unit, such as cents: a price of 4.35 becomes 435, sums and products of whole numbers are exact, and the conversion to a display format happens once, at the edge. A field in a body would then be named something like `price_cents`, so that nobody has to guess the unit.

diagram.alt: Two ways to hold money. As floating point, 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 and 4.35 x 100 is 434.99999999999994. As integer cents, 10 + 20 is 30 and 435 x 100 is 43500.
diagram.caption: Whole numbers of cents never drift, and decimal fractions can. Use the buttons to compare.

cases.label: As decimals

cases.label: As cents
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 300"><defs><marker id="mcents" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="4" orient="auto"><path class="f-ink" d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z"/></marker></defs><text class="t-bold" x="320" y="40" text-anchor="middle">Integer minor units</text><rect class="f-green-soft s-green w2" x="24" y="64" width="592" height="52" rx="8"/><text class="t-big" x="320" y="98" text-anchor="middle">10 + 20  =  30</text><rect class="f-green-soft s-green w2" x="24" y="140" width="592" height="52" rx="8"/><text class="t-big" x="320" y="174" text-anchor="middle">435 x 100 = 43500</text><text class="t" x="320" y="236" text-anchor="middle">Whole numbers of cents add up exactly.</text><text class="t-muted" x="320" y="266" text-anchor="middle">Convert to dollars only when displaying.</text></svg>

reveal.text: Both the conversion and the multiplication involve whole numbers only, so the result cannot drift.

lead.text: A 64-bit float has 53 bits to store the digits of a number, so it can hold every integer up to 2^53, which is 9007199254740992, and above that it can hold only some of them. The integer 9007199254740993 is not one of those, so a parser that reads it as a double returns 9007199254740992, and the id silently becomes a different id.

Database ids, such as 64-bit integers, can exceed that limit, and a client that parses them with a double will confuse neighbouring ids. The safe design is to send an identifier that may be large as a string, "9007199254740993", which no parser will round.

steps.headline: Decide whether the id 9007199254740993 survives being read as a double.

workedSteps.text: A double stores integers exactly up to 2^53, which is 9007199254740992.
The id is larger than the limit, so it lies beyond the range where every integer can be held.
The parser reads the nearest value that the double can hold, which is the limit itself.
Send the id as a string, and the digits arrive unchanged.

reveal.text: A server that conflated the three states could not tell a clear from a skipped field.

lessons.orientation: Judge whether text is valid JSON, design a response body, and handle money and large numbers safely.
lessons.nextAction: Read an OpenAPI description and check a body against its schema.

blocks.text: What a server sends when a client asks for order 42 is text such as `{"id": "42", "item": "pen", "qty": 3}`, because the order itself cannot travel over a network. That text is a **representation**, an encoding of the order's current state, and the encoding most APIs use is JSON, which a program reads by following a strict grammar and then either accepts the whole text or rejects it.
A person forgives a stray character and a parser does not, so the rules for writing a body are stricter than they first appear.

diagram.alt: A client sends GET /orders/42 with an Accept header. The server answers 200 OK with a Content-Type that matches and a body holding the same order, as JSON in one view and as XML in the other.
diagram.caption: The resource is the same in both views, and only its encoding changes. Use the buttons to change the Accept header.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to judge whether text is valid JSON, design a response body with stable names and types, and handle money and large integers safely.
intro.whyItMatters: A body is read by programs, and they are less forgiving than people.

recap.keyIdea: JSON is a strict text format, and a body should use stable names, integer minor units for money, strings for ids beyond 2^53, and separate states for absent, null and empty.

blocks.text: You saw that a representation is one encoding of a resource, chosen with Accept and declared in Content-Type, and that JSON rejects trailing commas, single quotes and leading zeros. You held money as integer cents because binary floating point cannot hold 0.1 exactly, and sent very large integers as strings for the same reason.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson writes the shape of an API down in OpenAPI, so that clients and servers can be checked against one description.

lessons.title: Describing an API with OpenAPI

lead.text: The document in the figure is an **OpenAPI document**: a description of an HTTP API that a tool can read. The format began as Swagger, and its specification was later donated to the Linux Foundation and renamed the OpenAPI Specification.

Used this way the description is a **contract**, and it does a job that prose cannot: the team writing the interface to the server and the team writing the client can both start from it at the same time.

diagram.caption: The whole interface of this small API fits in one document. Use the buttons to look at its three parts.

lead.text: Every OpenAPI document starts with the same few top-level parts, as the first view of the contract figure earlier in the lesson shows: the version of the format, **info** about the API, **paths**, and **components** for pieces that are used more than once. Under paths, each URL lists the methods it accepts, and each method is an **operation**.

Read the operation `POST /orders` line by line. Its **operationId**, `createOrder`, is a unique name that code generators turn into a function. Its **requestBody** points to the schema `Order`, and its **responses** list the status codes it can return, here 201 Created and 400 Invalid body. The responses matter as much as the body: documenting only the success case leaves the client to find the errors in production.

reveal.text: That name has to be unique across the whole document, so that two operations never produce the same function.

lead.text: A **schema** describes the allowed shape of a JSON value. The `Order` schema says that the value is an object, that it has the properties `item`, a string, and `qty`, an integer, and that both are listed under **required**. A body is valid when each required property is present *and* every property that is present has its declared type. Properties that the schema does not list are allowed, unless it says otherwise.

Two ideas are separate. **Required** concerns whether a property has to be present, and *nullable* concerns whether its value may be `null`, so a property can be required and still be allowed to hold `null`. A schema is also written once, under `components`, and reused with a **$ref** pointer wherever it is needed, which keeps each description in a single place.

steps.headline: Read the operation POST /orders from the document in the first figure.

workedSteps.text: The path is `/orders` and the method is `post`, so the operation is `POST /orders`.
Its `operationId` is `createOrder`, so a generated client has a function with that name.
Its `requestBody` refers to `Order`, which requires `item` and `qty`.
Under responses it lists the status codes the operation can return.

lead.text: A description of an API that lists only the successful response describes half of its behaviour. The 400 Invalid body response of `POST /orders` is just as much a part of the contract, and so are the 404 for a missing resource and the 401 and 403 of the earlier lesson.

If the `Order` schema is also the body of a `PUT` and the content of a response, it is written once under `components` and referenced with `$ref` in each place, so a change to the shape is made once and every operation follows it.

reveal.text: A validator reports one entry for each fault, and the client can fix them all in one pass.

lessons.orientation: Read an OpenAPI description to find paths, operations, required fields and documented responses, and check a request body against a schema.
lessons.nextAction: Page through a large collection without skipping or repeating rows.

blocks.text: A description of the operation `POST /orders`, written as data and not as prose, says that the operation is called `createOrder`, that its request body must match a schema named `Order`, which requires an item and a quantity, and that it answers either 201 or 400. A file of such descriptions is an **OpenAPI document**, and because a program can read it as easily as a person can, the same file can produce reference documentation, a client library in any language, a mock server and a set of tests.

A page of documentation can be misread, whereas a description can be checked: a request body either matches its schema or it does not, and a server whose answers differ from the file is shown to be wrong.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read an OpenAPI description for its paths, operations, required fields and responses, and check a request body against a schema.
intro.whyItMatters: A written contract lets two teams work at once and lets tools find mistakes.

recap.keyIdea: An OpenAPI document is a machine-readable contract: each operation names its input and its responses, and a schema states which properties are required and what type each has.

blocks.text: You read the skeleton of an OpenAPI document and followed one operation from its `operationId` to its documented responses. You then checked bodies against a schema, in which every required property must be present and every present property must have its type, and saw that error responses belong in the contract.

lessons.title: Pagination and filtering

lead.text: The simplest scheme uses two query parameters: **limit**, the number of items to return, and **offset**, the number to skip first. In the figure, 137 orders at 25 to a page give `?limit=25&offset=0` for the first page and `?limit=25&offset=125` for the last, and that last page holds only 12 items.

The number of pages is the item count divided by the page size, *rounded up*, because a partly filled page is still a page. For 137 items it is 137 / 25 = 5.48, which is 6 pages. The offset for page n is (n - 1) x limit, so the sixth page starts at 5 x 25 = 125.

diagram.alt: A bar of 137 items divided into six pages: five pages of 25 items and a last page of 12. One page is highlighted, with the offset parameter that fetches it.
diagram.caption: The offset says how many items to skip, and the limit says how many to return. Use the buttons to see the first and the last page.

The next screen shows the same effect with ten rows, and a way to avoid it.

lead.text: An offset counts from the start of the list, so it is only right while the start stays where it was. In the figure, ids 100 down to 91 are listed newest first, and page 1 has returned 100 to 96. Then 101 and 102 arrive at the top. The list now begins 102, 101, 100, and the five rows from offset 5 are 97, 96, 95, 94 and 93: 97 and 96 appear a second time. Rows deleted from the front have the opposite effect, and rows are skipped.

**Keyset paging** asks for the rows that come *after the last one the client saw*. The request `?limit=5&after=96` returns 95, 94, 93, 92 and 91, whatever has been added above. It also costs less, because the database can start at the key in an index and does not have to count and discard the skipped rows.

diagram.alt: A list of twelve cards, ids 102 down to 91, after two new rows, 102 and 101, were added at the top. With offset paging the second page, offset 5, contains 97 and 96, which were on the first page. With keyset paging, after 96, the second page is 95 down to 91.

reveal.text: The page never contains the key itself, only the rows after it.

lead.text: A keyset request needs the last key the client saw, and an API usually hides this in a **cursor**, a token that the client receives with each page and sends back for the next.

A cursor is **opaque**. Because the client treats it as a string to hand back, the server may add a sort key, a filter or a signature later without breaking anyone, and may refuse a cursor that has been altered.

The page starts one place later, at position 5.
Take `limit = 5` rows from there.
Those rows are 95, 94, 93, 92 and 91.

lead.text: Narrowing and ordering a list are also done with the query: `?status=open&sort=-created&limit=20` asks for open orders, newest first. A server should accept only the filters and sorts it documents, since a free-form query handed to the database is an invitation to injection.

If several orders share a creation time, their relative order is not fixed, and a cursor that records only the time cannot say which of them comes next. The usual remedy is to sort by the pair of the time and the unique id, so that every row has exactly one place.

reveal.text: Adding the id to the sort gives every row a unique place, which a cursor can name.

lessons.orientation: Compute offset pages, show how offset paging repeats items when data changes, and implement keyset paging.
lessons.nextAction: Shape an error response with problem details, and make a POST safe to retry with an idempotency key.

blocks.text: A list of 137 orders returned in a single response grows with every new order, and sooner or later it is too large to send before the client gives up. The usual remedy is to return the list in pages and to ask for each page by the position at which it begins: with pages of 25 the first begins at position 0 and the sixth at position 125. That position is called an **offset**, and the sixth page holds only 12 orders, since 137 is not a multiple of 25.

An offset is exact only while the list stays still, and a list of orders does not. When a new order arrives at the front, every later row moves down one place, so a client that counts from the start may no longer begin where it left off.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count offset pages, predict which rows a changing list repeats, and page with a key and a cursor.
intro.whyItMatters: Every list endpoint needs paging, and the way it is done decides whether rows are skipped or repeated.

recap.keyIdea: Offset paging counts from the start and repeats or skips rows when the list changes, whereas keyset paging resumes after a key and a cursor hides that key from the client.

blocks.text: You counted pages as the item count divided by the page size, rounded up, and saw that rows inserted at the front push an offset onto rows already read. Keyset paging avoids this by asking for rows after a known key, a cursor keeps that key opaque, and a sort needs a unique tiebreaker.

lessons.title: Errors and safe retries

reveal.text: The next screens explain why a retry of a POST is dangerous, and what the server can do about it.

lead.text: A payment is made with a POST, and it is the case where a retry costs the most. In the figure the first view shows what happens when the client resends the charge: the response was lost, so the first charge had gone through, and the second charge is made on top of it.

A rule that the client should not retry does not solve this, because a charge that is lost really does need another attempt. The answer is to let the server recognise a repeat. The effect of a request then happens *once*, even though the request may arrive many times, and this is a property that the server has to supply.

diagram.alt: Four steps for a charge of 20 against a balance of 80. The response to the first request is lost and the client sends it again. Without a key the server charges twice and the balance is 40. With a key it recognises the repeat and the balance stays at 60.
diagram.caption: The only difference between the two views is the key. Use the buttons to compare them.

lead.text: With an **idempotency key**, the client generates a unique value for each logical operation, such as a random identifier, and sends it in a header, conventionally named `Idempotency-Key`. The first time the server sees the key it carries out the request and stores the result under that key. When the key arrives again, from a retry, it does not act: it returns the stored response, as in the second view of the figure on the previous screen.

The same key must always mean the same request, so the server stores a **fingerprint** of the body along with the key and the response. A repeat with the same key and the same fingerprint gets the stored response. A repeat with the same key and a different body is a mistake by the client, and the server rejects it, commonly with 422 or 409. A header of this name is widely used, and the IETF has a draft to standardise it, which was not yet an RFC when this was written.

reveal.text: Retries become harmless, which is what lets a client send them freely after a timeout.

lead.text: The key should be scoped to the client that sent it, so that two clients who happen to pick the same value do not collide, and to the operation it was sent with. The server keeps it for long enough to cover the retries a client might make, such as a day, and then discards it, since storing every key for ever is expensive.
It is the first sight of a key that acts, which is why the total charged by a server depends on the number of *distinct* keys and not on the number of requests.

reveal.text: The repeated requests for x and y are recognised as retries.

steps.headline: Apply the rule to the requests (k1, 40), (k2, 10) and (k1, 40), in that order.

workedSteps.text: The key k1 has not been seen, so the server charges 40 and stores the result.
The key k2 has not been seen either, so the server charges 10.
The key k1 arrives again, and the server has already stored a result under it.
The third request is returned the stored response from the first, and the total charged is 50.

steps.headline: Apply the rule to the requests (p, 25), (q, 5), (p, 25) and (r, 10).

workedSteps.text: The keys p and q are new, so 25 and 5 are charged.
The third request carries p again, and the fourth carries r.
The total charged is the sum of what the server acted on.

lead.text: A status code says that a request failed, and the body should say why. RFC 9457 defines a JSON shape for this, served with the media type **application/problem+json**, which it calls **problem details**. Its members, as the figure shows, are **type**, a URI that identifies the kind of error, **title**, a short name for it, **status**, the HTTP status code, **detail**, an explanation of this occurrence, and optionally **instance**, an identifier for this occurrence.

A client reacts to the *type*, which stays the same however the wording changes, and a person reads the title and the detail. The detail should say what the client can fix, and it should never carry a stack trace, a SQL statement or a file path, since those help an attacker and belong in the server's own logs.

The full trace goes to the server's log, where the developers can see it and an attacker cannot.

lessons.orientation: Shape an error response with problem details, and make a POST safe to retry with an idempotency key.
lessons.nextAction: Tell a change that breaks clients from one that does not, and deprecate something safely.

blocks.text: A header named `Idempotency-Key`, carrying a unique value that the client chooses for each operation, lets a server recognise that a `POST` it has received is a repeat of one it has already carried out, and answer with the stored result instead of acting a second time. Without an **idempotency key** a client that retries a charge after a timeout has no safe way to ask again, because nothing in a plain `POST` tells the server whether it has met this request before.
An error body with a stable, machine-readable type and a short explanation lets a client decide what to do and lets a person see what happened, and RFC 9457 defines a JSON shape for it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to shape an error response with problem details, and make a POST safe to retry with an idempotency key.
intro.whyItMatters: A request that may arrive more than once has to be made safe by the server.

recap.keyIdea: An idempotency key lets a server recognise a repeated POST and return the stored result, and an error body should give a stable type for programs and a detail for people.

blocks.text: You compared a charge delivered three times without a key, which leaves 10, with the same charge under a key, which leaves 70. The server stores the key, a fingerprint of the body and the response, and rejects a reused key with a different body. A problem-details body carries a type, title, status, detail and optionally an instance, and shows no internals.

lessons.title: Versioning and change

reveal.text: The next screens set out the test, and the figure sorts changes into three groups.

lead.text: The owners of an API usually cannot update its clients, so every change is judged against what a client built on the old contract does with it. A change is **breaking** if any such client can fail.

Three kinds of change break clients: removing or renaming a field they read, changing its type, and making a request field required that callers used to leave out. An **additive** change, such as a new optional field in a response, a new endpoint or a new optional query parameter, breaks nothing, because a client ignores what it has never heard of. Additive changes therefore need no new version.

The first two lists in the figure follow from the test. The third list holds the changes that deserve a second look. An **enum** is a field whose value comes from a fixed list, such as an order status of `"new"`, `"paid"` or `"shipped"`, and a client that handles each known value with a case of its own may fail on a new one, so adding a value is safe only if clients have been told to expect more. Tightening validation, for instance lowering the longest allowed name from 200 characters to 50, rejects requests that used to work. Changing the default sort order changes what a client that never asked for a sort receives.

The remedy for the first of these, a new enum value, is a convention that is written down in the contract: **clients ignore what they do not recognise**. A client that follows it is a **tolerant reader**, and it is what makes additive change safe in practice.

diagram.alt: Three lists of API changes: safe changes such as adding an optional response field, breaking changes such as renaming a field, and subtle changes such as adding an enum value.
diagram.caption: A change is judged by what an existing client does with the new response or request. Use the buttons to read each list.

Clients that never read the field are not affected, whatever else changes.

lead.text: Renaming `qty` to `quantity` can be done without breaking anyone, if the old name is kept for a period. The server first returns **both** fields and announces that `qty` is **deprecated**, meaning that it will be removed, with a date. A response header named **Deprecation** says that the field or endpoint is deprecated, and a header named **Sunset** carries the date on which it will stop working, so that a client can find out from its own traffic.

The server then measures how many calls still read the old field. In the figure that count falls from 12,000 a day when the notice goes out to 300 after the date, and the field is removed when nobody depends on it. Putting a version in the URL, as in `/v2/orders`, or in a header changes only where the two contracts are named. In either design the real work is to keep both of them running until the clients have moved.

diagram.alt: Four stages of renaming a response field from qty to quantity: announce, serve both fields, pass the Sunset date, and remove the old field. A bar shows example traffic still using qty, falling from 12,000 calls a day to none.
diagram.caption: The old field stays until nobody reads it. Use the buttons to step through the migration.

steps.headline: Rename qty to quantity in a response without breaking a client.

workedSteps.text: Add quantity to every response, holding the same value as qty.
Keep qty in the response as well, for the whole migration.
Announce the deprecation of qty, with a Sunset date, and watch the traffic that still reads it.
When no calls read qty, remove it. Clients that moved to quantity are unaffected.

steps.headline: Check a new response against an old one. Old fields: id (integer), name (string). New fields: id (string), name (string), nick (string).

workedSteps.text: Every old field must still be present: id and name both are.
Every present field must have its old type. name is still a string, and nick is only an addition.
The last old field to check is id, which was an integer.

reveal.text: A mechanical check on every old field would catch each of these before release.

lessons.orientation: Classify a change to an API as breaking or non-breaking, and describe how to evolve an API without stranding clients.
lessons.nextAction: Tell authentication from authorisation, and explain how sessions, tokens and password hashing work.

blocks.text: Renaming the field `name` to `full_name` in a response such as `{"id": 7, "name": "Ana"}` takes a moment, and every program that was written to read `name` finds nothing there afterwards. The programs that read it may be apps on phones, scripts on other companies' servers and tools that nobody remembers writing, and the team that owns the API cannot update any of them on demand. A change is **breaking** when a client written against the old contract can fail because of it.
A team can still make a breaking change by running a migration, which keeps the old form working for a period that it announces, until nobody depends on it.

diagram.alt: A server response with the fields id and name, read by an installed app that expects both. After the server renames name to full_name, the app cannot find name and fails.
diagram.caption: The server changed and the app did not. Use the buttons to see the response before and after the rename.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to classify a change as breaking or non-breaking, and describe how to move an API forward without stranding its clients.
intro.whyItMatters: An API is promised to clients you cannot update, so every change has to be judged from their side.

recap.keyIdea: A change is breaking when an old client can fail, and a breaking change is made safely by serving old and new together, announcing a Sunset date and removing the old form once nobody uses it.

blocks.text: Removing or renaming a field, changing its type and newly requiring a request field are breaking, while additions are not, provided clients ignore what they do not recognise. A migration keeps both forms, announces the date with Deprecation and Sunset headers, watches the traffic and then removes the old form.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to security, and begins by asking who is calling an API and whether they may.

lessons.title: Identity, sessions and tokens

reveal.text: The reply depends on which of the two questions failed.

lead.text: **Authentication** asks *who is calling*, and the caller answers with a password, an API key, a token or a certificate. **Authorisation** asks *whether this caller may do this*, which depends on what they are asking for. The two failures get different codes, as the status lesson showed: a request that cannot be tied to a caller gets 401, and a request from a known caller who is not allowed gets 403.

A caller has to prove who they are on every request, and HTTP keeps no memory between requests, so something has to be carried each time. There are two common designs: a **session**, where the server remembers, and a **token**, where the request carries its own proof.

After a successful login the server creates a **session**: it makes a long random id, stores it in a table next to the user it belongs to, and sends the id to the client in a **cookie**, a small value the browser returns with every later request to the same site. On a later request the server reads the id from the cookie, looks it up and finds user 7.

The id is the only thing the client holds, so anyone who copies it is logged in as that user, and three cookie attributes limit the risk. **HttpOnly** keeps the cookie out of reach of scripts in the page, **Secure** makes the browser send it only over HTTPS, and **SameSite** restricts when it is sent along with requests that start on other sites. The cost of a session is the lookup, since every request needs the table.

diagram.alt: A login creates a session on the server and returns its id in a cookie. A later request carries the cookie, and the server looks the id up to find the user.
diagram.caption: The client holds an id and the server holds the state. Use the buttons to step from login to a later request.

reveal.text: The id then reaches the server on requests, and the page's own scripts never see it.

lead.text: A **signed token** puts the facts, such as `user=7`, in the token itself, and adds a signature that only the server can produce. The signature is an **HMAC**, a hash of the payload mixed with a secret key that only the server knows. To check a token the server recomputes the HMAC of the payload with its key and compares the result with the signature that arrived. Altering one character of the payload gives a completely different HMAC, and so the old signature no longer matches.

Two warnings go with this. The payload is only *encoded*, usually with base64, and anyone who holds the token can decode it, so a secret must never be put in a token. And the comparison should be done in **constant time**, with a function such as `hmac.compare_digest` in Python, because the `==` operator stops at the first byte that differs, and an attacker can measure how long it took.

diagram.alt: A token with payload user=7 and a signature. The server computes the HMAC of the payload with its secret key and compares it with the signature sent. If the payload is changed to user=8 and the signature is not, the computed value differs and the token is rejected.
diagram.caption: The signature protects the payload from change, and does not hide it. Use the buttons to compare a genuine token with an altered one.
