questions.prompt: A balance is 100. A client sends `POST /charges` for 30 with the same Idempotency-Key three times, two of them retries, and the server stores the result under the key. What is the balance afterwards?
hints: Only the first delivery acts.
The repeats return the stored response.
One charge of 30 comes off the balance.
questions.onCorrect: The repeats are recognised by their key, so only one charge is made.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the balance without a key, where all three deliveries act.
That is the amount charged, not the balance.

questions.prompt: Which media type does RFC 9457 give for a problem-details body?
hints: It starts with application.
It names the problem format and JSON.
questions.onCorrect: The media type lets a client recognise the body as a problem-details object before it reads any member.

misconceptions.feedback: A plain JSON type would not tell a client that the body is a problem description. RFC 9457 defines a more specific type.

questions.prompt: A server charges the amount of a request on the first sight of its key and ignores repeats. It receives, in order, (a, 30), (a, 30), (b, 20), (a, 30). How much is charged in total?
hints: Key a is seen three times.
Only the first sight of a key is charged.
Add the amounts for a and b once each.
questions.onCorrect: The repeats of a are ignored, so a and b are each charged once.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every request. Repeats of a key are ignored.
The key a is charged once, and not twice.

questions.prompt: Which change is non-breaking for existing clients?
hints: Ask whether an old client could still do everything it did before.
Three of the four take something away or demand something new.

acceptedIdeas: Adding an optional field to a response
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Adding an optional field to a response

questions.onCorrect: An old client reads the fields it knows and ignores a field it has never heard of, so an addition leaves it working.

misconceptions.feedback: A client that reads the old name will no longer find it.
A client that treats id as an integer will fail on a string.
Callers who leave the field out would now be refused.

choices.label: Changing id from integer to string
Renaming a response field
Adding an optional field to a response
Making an optional request field required

questions.prompt: Five changes are proposed. (a) add an optional response field `nick`. (b) remove the response field `name`. (c) change `id` from integer to string. (d) add the endpoint `/orders/{id}/notes`. (e) make the request field `currency` required, though it was optional. How many are breaking?
hints: Ask for each change whether an old client could fail.
Removing, retyping and newly requiring are the three kinds to look for.
Additions do not break old clients.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (b), (c) and (e) are breaking, and (a) and (d) are additions: 3.

questions.onCorrect: Removing a field, changing its type and making a request field required each make a client written against the old contract fail.

misconceptions.feedback: Count each of removal, retyping and the newly required request field.
Two of the five are additions, which do not break clients.

questions.prompt: Five client apps use an API. Three read the field qty, and two read only id and name. The server removes qty and adds quantity in the same version. How many clients fail?
hints: Which clients depend on the removed field?
Clients that do not read it keep working.
Count the clients that read qty.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The three clients that read qty fail, and the two that do not keep working: 3.

questions.onCorrect: A client fails exactly when it relies on something that is gone, so the number of failures equals the number of clients that read the field.

misconceptions.feedback: The two clients that read only id and name do not depend on qty, so they keep working.
It is the three clients that read qty that fail.

questions.prompt: During the migration the response carries both the old field qty and the new field quantity. How many fields in the response hold the quantity?
hints: The old field stays, and the new one is added.
Both are served during the deprecation period.
Count them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: qty and quantity are both present: 2 fields.

questions.onCorrect: Serving both lets old clients keep reading qty while new clients move to quantity.

misconceptions.feedback: During the migration the old field is kept as well as the new one.
There is one old field and one new field.

questions.prompt: Old response fields are id (integer) and name (string). The new response has id (string), name (string) and nick (string). How many old fields fail the compatibility check, because they are missing or have a different type?
hints: Compare each old field with the field of the same name in the new response.
name is unchanged.
Look at the type of id.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only id changed type, from integer to string: 1 field fails.

questions.onCorrect: Extra fields in the new response are fine, since a tolerant client ignores them, but each old field must remain with its type.

misconceptions.feedback: One of the old fields has a different type in the new response.
nick is new and is not an old field, so it cannot fail the check.

questions.prompt: An old response has six fields: id, name, qty, price, note and status. The new one drops note, renames status to state, changes price from an integer to a string, and adds a field tags. How many old fields fail the check?
hints: A field fails if it is missing or its type changed.
note is gone, and so is status under that name.
Do not count the field that was added.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: note is missing, status is missing and price changed type: 3.

questions.onCorrect: Each old field is checked for presence and type, and adding tags breaks nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: The new field tags is an addition and does not fail the check.
price changed type, and note and status are missing: that makes three.

questions.prompt: Seven changes are proposed. (a) add the endpoint /reports. (b) add an optional response field. (c) rename a response field. (d) make an optional request field required. (e) change a field from integer to string. (f) add an optional query parameter. (g) lower the allowed length of a request field from 200 to 50 characters. How many are breaking?
hints: Renaming, newly requiring and retyping are breaking.
Tightening validation can refuse requests that used to work.
Additions of an endpoint, a field or an optional parameter are not breaking.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (c), (d), (e) and (g) are breaking: 4.

questions.onCorrect: A tighter limit rejects requests that were valid, so (g) breaks clients that send them, as do (c), (d) and (e).

misconceptions.feedback: Tightening the validation also rejects requests that used to be accepted.
Three of the seven are additions, which do not break clients.

questions.prompt: A response field qty is removed and replaced by quantity in the same version. Which clients fail?
hints: Who depends on the field that is gone?
The language of the client is not the issue.
questions.onCorrect: Any client that reads qty finds nothing there, whatever language it is written in.

misconceptions.feedback: JSON gives a client no way to find a field that has been removed.
A client in any language that reads the missing field fails, or gets nothing.
The method a client uses to send is not what matters. It is the field it reads.

choices.label: Clients that read qty
Only clients that send POST
Only clients written in statically typed languages
None, because JSON is flexible

questions.prompt: Which response header gives the date after which a deprecated feature will stop working?
hints: It is one of the two headers that announce a deprecation.
The other one, Deprecation, says that the feature is deprecated. This one gives the date.
questions.onCorrect: A Sunset header gives clients a date to plan against, and a measure of the traffic that remains shows whether the date is safe.

misconceptions.feedback: The Deprecation header announces that something is deprecated. The one that gives the date it goes away is a different header.

questions.prompt: A request has no token at all. Which status code is correct?
hints: Is the caller identified at all?
The status that is about missing or invalid credentials.
questions.onCorrect: 401 reports missing or invalid credentials. 403 is for a caller who is identified and not permitted.

misconceptions.feedback: A 200 would tell the client that the request succeeded, and nothing has been authenticated.
403 is for a caller who is known and refused. This caller is not known.
404 says that nothing exists at the address, which is not what is wrong.

questions.prompt: Which cookie attribute stops JavaScript running in the page from reading the cookie?
hints: Its name says it is for HTTP and not for scripts.
It is one of Secure, SameSite and this one.
questions.onCorrect: HttpOnly keeps the session id out of scripts, so a script injected into the page cannot steal it.

misconceptions.feedback: Secure makes the browser send the cookie only over HTTPS. The attribute that hides it from scripts is another one.
SameSite limits when the cookie is sent with cross-site requests. It does not hide it from scripts.

questions.prompt: HMAC-SHA256 produces 256 bits. Written in hex, with four bits to a digit, how many characters is the digest?
hints: One hex digit stands for four bits.
Divide the number of bits by four.
256 divided by four.
questions.onCorrect: A hex digit holds four bits, so a 256-bit digest takes 64 hex characters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the digest length in bytes. Each byte takes two hex characters.
That is the number of bits. Each hex digit stands for four.

questions.prompt: A token carries the payload `user=8` with the signature made for `user=7`. The server verifies it and finds the signatures differ. Which status code should it send?
hints: The token cannot be trusted as credentials.
Is the caller authenticated?
The code for missing or invalid credentials.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The signature does not match, so the credentials are invalid: 401.

questions.onCorrect: A token that fails verification is invalid credentials, and the response is 401.

misconceptions.feedback: 403 says the caller is identified but not allowed. A token that fails verification does not identify anyone.
The request was well formed. The credentials in it are what is invalid.

questions.prompt: A 6-digit PIN has 10^6 possible values. An attacker makes 1,000 guesses per second. How many seconds does it take to try every one?
hints: The number of values is 1,000,000.
Divide it by the guesses per second.
Divide the total by one thousand.
questions.onCorrect: Guessing time is the number of possibilities divided by the guessing rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of possible PINs. Divide it by the number of guesses made each second.
At a thousand guesses a second the thousand-fold gap is not that large.

questions.prompt: A password hash is made 100 times slower, so the attacker manages 10 guesses per second instead of 1,000. How many seconds does it now take to try all 10^6 PINs?
hints: The number of possibilities is unchanged.
Divide it by the new rate.
1,000,000 divided by 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1,000,000 / 10 = 100,000 seconds, which is 100 times longer.

questions.onCorrect: A slow hash cuts the attacker's rate, and the time grows by the same factor.

misconceptions.feedback: That was the time at 1,000 guesses a second. The rate is now 10.
Divide the number of values by 10 guesses per second.

questions.prompt: A token's payload is the base64 encoding of `{"user": 7, "role": "admin"}`, followed by an HMAC signature. Who can read the payload?
hints: Is base64 encryption?
What does the key protect?
questions.onCorrect: Base64 is a reversible encoding, so the payload is readable by anyone, and the key protects only against changes.

misconceptions.feedback: Encoding is not encryption, and anyone can decode base64 without a key.
A token can pass through other hands, and nothing in it hides the payload.
The secret key signs the token, and it does not hide the payload.

choices.label: Nobody without the secret key
Only the server, because it is encoded
Only the user it belongs to
Anyone who holds the token

questions.prompt: There are 26^8 = 208,827,064,576 possible 8-letter lowercase passwords. An attacker makes 1,000 guesses per second. About how many days does it take to try them all, rounded to a whole number?
hints: Divide the number of passwords by 1,000 for seconds.
Divide seconds by 86,400, the seconds in a day.
The result is a little under two and a half thousand.
questions.onCorrect: A day has 86,400 seconds, so the days are the seconds divided by 86,400.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of seconds. Divide it by 86,400 to convert to days.
The scale is off by a thousand. Check the division by 1,000.

questions.prompt: Which Python function compares two signatures in constant time, so that timing does not reveal how many bytes matched?
hints: It lives in the hmac module.
Its name says it compares digests.
questions.onCorrect: A comparison with `==` stops at the first difference, and its timing can leak how many leading bytes matched.

misconceptions.feedback: The `==` operator stops at the first difference, so its timing can leak how much of a signature was right.

questions.prompt: Why is a fast hash such as plain SHA-256 a poor way to store passwords?
hints: Speed helps both sides.
A stolen table lets an attacker guess offline.

acceptedIdeas: It lets an attacker who steals the table try guesses very quickly
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It lets an attacker who steals the table try guesses very quickly

questions.onCorrect: Speed helps the attacker as much as the owner, so a password hash should be slow and salted, such as Argon2id.

misconceptions.feedback: The length of the output is not the weakness.
A server can run any hash. The weakness is how fast an attacker can too.
A hash does not decide whether passwords are case sensitive.

choices.label: It produces hashes that are too long
It makes passwords case sensitive
It lets an attacker who steals the table try guesses very quickly
It cannot be run on a server

questions.prompt: The `users` table has 3 rows. A handler builds `SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '<input>'` by joining strings, and receives the input `x' OR '1'='1`. How many rows come back?
hints: Write out the query that results from the join.
The condition `'1'='1'` is always true.
An OR with a true condition matches every row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The final condition is true for every row, so all 3 rows come back.

questions.onCorrect: The input closes the string and adds a condition that is true for every row, so the query returns the whole table.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the result when the input stays a value, as in a parameterised query. Here the input becomes part of the query.
The added condition is true for every row, so the filter on name no longer narrows anything.

questions.prompt: The `users` table has 3 rows. A handler runs `SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?` with the value `x' OR '1'='1` as a parameter. How many rows come back?
hints: The whole input is treated as one string value.
Is there a user whose name is exactly that string?
Count the matching rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: No user has that exact name, so no rows are returned: 0.

questions.onCorrect: A parameter is always data, so the query compares the name with the whole string and finds nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That would happen if the input became part of the query text. A parameter never does.
The input is a single value, and no row has a name equal to it.

questions.prompt: `GET /invoices/{id}` returns an invoice whenever the caller is logged in. Which fix addresses the flaw?
hints: The flaw is that any logged-in caller can ask for any invoice.
Which change refuses a caller who does not own it?

acceptedIdeas: Check that the invoice belongs to the caller before returning it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Check that the invoice belongs to the caller before returning it

questions.onCorrect: The server has to compare the owner of the object with the caller on every request.

misconceptions.feedback: Longer ids make guessing harder, but an id that leaks is still accepted. The server has to check ownership.
A hidden link does not stop a request. The server enforces the rule, not the interface.
HTTPS protects the data in transit. It does not decide whose invoice it is.

choices.label: Hide the invoice link in the interface
Check that the invoice belongs to the caller before returning it
Make invoice ids longer
Require HTTPS

questions.prompt: A request body is `{"name": "Ana", "role": "admin", "email": "a@x"}` and the allowlist is `name` and `email`. How many fields are copied onto the stored user?
hints: Only keys in the allowlist are copied.
role is not in the allowlist.
Count the keys that are.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: name and email are allowed, and role is not: 2 fields are copied.

questions.onCorrect: An allowlist names the fields a caller may set, and everything else is dropped or rejected.

misconceptions.feedback: The field role is not in the allowlist, so it is not copied.
Both name and email are in the allowlist.

questions.prompt: Invoice 18 belongs to user 4, and user 9 is the caller. Which user's id must the handler compare with the caller's? Give the id.
hints: The handler loads the invoice first.
The owner is stored on the invoice.
The invoice belongs to the user named in the question.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The owner of invoice 18 is user 4, and the caller is user 9, which differ.

questions.onCorrect: The handler loads the object and compares its owner with the authenticated caller.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the caller. The check compares the caller with the owner of the object.
That is the invoice id, not the user who owns it.

questions.prompt: A payload has the keys name, nick, email, role, id and balance, and the allowlist is name, email and nick. How many fields are copied in all?
hints: Check each key against the allowlist.
role, id and balance are not on the list.
Count the keys that are.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: name, nick and email are allowed: 3 fields.

questions.onCorrect: Only the allowlisted keys reach the stored object, so role, id and balance are dropped.

misconceptions.feedback: Only keys on the allowlist are copied, and role, id and balance are not on it.
All of name, nick and email are on the list.

questions.prompt: Invoices 17, 18, 19 and 20 belong to users 4, 9, 4 and 9 in that order. User 9 requests all four, and the handler checks the owner on each request. How many invoices are returned?
hints: Check the owner of each invoice against user 9.
Invoices 18 and 20 belong to user 9.
The others are refused.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: User 9 owns invoices 18 and 20, so 2 are returned.

questions.onCorrect: With the check in place, a caller gets only the objects they own.

misconceptions.feedback: Without the owner check all four would be returned. With it, only user 9's own invoices are.
User 9 owns some of the invoices, and those are returned.

questions.prompt: The `users` table has 7 rows. A handler builds `SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '<input>'` by joining strings, and receives the input `x' OR '1'='1`. What comes back?
hints: The added condition is always true.
An OR with a true condition matches every row.
So the result is the whole table.
questions.onCorrect: The condition on the name no longer narrows the result, so every row is returned.

misconceptions.feedback: The added condition is true for every row, not for just one.
That is the result for a parameterised query. Here the input has become part of the query.

choices.label: One row
All seven rows
No rows

questions.prompt: Which is the dependable fix for injection into a database query?
hints: The fix has to keep data and code apart.
Hand escaping is easy to get wrong.

acceptedIdeas: Pass input as parameters of a parameterised query
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pass input as parameters of a parameterised query

questions.onCorrect: A parameter is always treated as a value and never as part of the query, whatever it contains.

misconceptions.feedback: Escaping by hand misses cases, and a single mistake reopens the flaw.
An error page hides symptoms and does not stop the query being changed.
A short input can still be harmful, such as `x' OR '1'='1`.

choices.label: Limit the length of every input
Show a generic error page
Remove quotation marks from the input by hand
Pass input as parameters of a parameterised query

questions.prompt: What is the flaw called when a handler copies every field of a request body onto a stored object, so that a caller can set fields such as role?
hints: The fix is an allowlist.
The name says that many fields are assigned at once.
questions.onCorrect: Accepting only an allowlist of fields means a caller cannot set role, id or balance.

misconceptions.feedback: Injection changes the structure of a query. Copying every field of a body onto an object is a different flaw.

questions.prompt: A token bucket has capacity 3, refills 1 token per second and starts full. Four requests arrive at t = 0. How many are allowed?
hints: The bucket starts with a token for each unit of capacity.
Each allowed request spends one token.
The refill adds nothing at t = 0.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three tokens allow three requests, and the fourth finds the bucket empty: 3.

questions.onCorrect: A full bucket allows a burst of its capacity, and the next request has to wait for the refill.

misconceptions.feedback: The bucket holds only three tokens at the start, and nothing has been added yet.
The bucket starts full, so a burst is allowed.

questions.prompt: A bucket has capacity 4, refills 2 tokens per second and starts full. Five requests arrive at t = 0 and one more at t = 1. How many of the six are allowed?
hints: At t = 0 the bucket holds 4 tokens.
By t = 1 the refill has added 2.
Count the allowed requests at t = 0, then at t = 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four are allowed at t = 0, the fifth is refused, and the refill to 2 tokens allows the sixth at t = 1: 5.

questions.onCorrect: The tokens fill again at the refill rate, up to the capacity, so a later request finds some.

misconceptions.feedback: At t = 1 the bucket has gained two tokens, which allow the last request.
The bucket holds four tokens at t = 0, so the fifth request at that moment is refused.

questions.prompt: A client sends idempotent requests and may retry. Which response is worth retrying after a short wait?
hints: Which fault might go away with time?
The other three will fail the same way again.
questions.onCorrect: A 503 reports a temporary condition at the server. The 4xx codes report faults that a wait does not repair.

misconceptions.feedback: The request is malformed, and sending it again will fail in the same way.
The resource is not there, and a wait does not create it.
The caller is not allowed, and waiting does not change that.

choices.label: 403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
503 Service Unavailable
400 Bad Request

questions.prompt: A client waits 150 ms before the first retry, and doubles the wait each time, with no cap. How many milliseconds does it wait before the fifth retry?
hints: The waits are 150, then doubled each time.
The fifth wait has been doubled four times.
150 times 2 to the fourth.
questions.onCorrect: The nth wait is the base multiplied by 2 to the power n - 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fourth wait. The fifth is double it.
That is the sixth wait. Count five waits from 150.

questions.prompt: A bucket with capacity 3 and a refill of 1 token per second was emptied at t = 0. How many tokens does it hold at t = 1, before the next request?
hints: Nothing is added between requests at the same instant.
One second has passed since the bucket was emptied.
The refill adds one token each second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0 + 1 x 1 = 1 token.

questions.onCorrect: Tokens return at the refill rate, up to the capacity, so one second brings one token.

misconceptions.feedback: The bucket refills gradually, at the refill rate, and does not jump back to full.
Time has passed since the bucket was emptied, so the refill has added something.

questions.prompt: A client retries six times, with waits of 300, 600, 1200 and 2400 ms and then 4000 ms twice, because the doubling is capped at 4000. What is the total waiting time in milliseconds?
hints: Add the six waits.
The fifth and sixth are 4000, not 4800 and 9600.
300 + 600 + 1200 + 2400 is the first four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4500 for the first four, plus 4000 twice: 12500 ms.

questions.onCorrect: The cap limits the fifth and sixth waits to 4000 ms, so the total is smaller than with doubling alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 4800 and 9600 for the last two waits. The cap holds each at 4000.
That is the total of the first five waits. The sixth adds another 4000.

questions.prompt: A client sent six idempotent requests and got these results: 200, 400, 429, 503, 404 and a timeout. How many of them are worth retrying after a wait?
hints: A 200 succeeded.
A 400 and a 404 will fail again.
The temporary conditions are worth another try.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 429, the 503 and the timeout are worth retrying: 3.

questions.onCorrect: Retry only what can change with time: timeouts, 429 and 503, and only for requests that are idempotent or carry a key.

misconceptions.feedback: The 200 succeeded, and the 400 and the 404 will fail in the same way again.
The timeout is also a failure that may clear with time.

questions.prompt: A bucket has capacity 2, refills 1 token per second and starts full. Requests arrive at t = 0, 0, 0, 1, 1 and 3 seconds. How many are allowed?
hints: Two are allowed at t = 0, and the third is refused.
At t = 1 the bucket has one token, and the second request there is refused.
By t = 3 the bucket has refilled to its capacity.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: t = 0: allow, allow, refuse. t = 1: allow, refuse. t = 3: allow. That is 4.

questions.onCorrect: Tokens are added at the refill rate and never above the capacity.

misconceptions.feedback: At t = 3 the bucket has refilled, so the last request is allowed.
Two of the requests find the bucket empty.

questions.prompt: A client retries four times with waits that start at 200 ms and double each time, with no cap. What is the total waiting time in milliseconds?
hints: The waits are 200, 400, and so on.
Double each wait to get the next.
Add the four waits.
questions.onCorrect: Each wait doubles, so the total is the first wait multiplied by 15.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fourth wait alone. The total includes all four.
That is only the third wait.

questions.prompt: Why do clients add random jitter to their retry delays?
hints: What happens when a thousand clients fail together?
Think about the load when the server comes back.

acceptedIdeas: So that many clients do not all retry at the same moment
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: So that many clients do not all retry at the same moment

questions.onCorrect: Clients that fail together would retry together, and jitter spreads those retries out.

misconceptions.feedback: Jitter does not change the cost of a retry. It changes when the retries arrive.
A retry succeeds only if the server can serve it, and jitter cannot guarantee that.
A 429 is the server's reply to an excess of requests. Jitter is a way to send fewer at a time.

choices.label: So that many clients do not all retry at the same moment
So that retries always succeed
To make each retry cheaper for the server
To avoid using a 429

questions.prompt: Where should the rule 'an order cannot ship before it is paid' live?
hints: The rule is about the business and not about HTTP or storage.
Which layer applies the rules?
questions.onCorrect: The service applies business rules, so they can be tested without a server and reused by any handler.

misconceptions.feedback: The handler translates HTTP to and from calls. A rule kept there would be lost when a second entry point is added.
The repository talks to storage. A business rule hidden in SQL cannot be tested on its own.
The client can be bypassed, so a rule kept there is not enforced.

choices.label: The repository SQL
The client
The service layer
The handler, as an if before the response

questions.prompt: Which layer turns a failure such as 'order not paid' into the status code 409?
hints: It is the layer that knows about HTTP.
It reads the request and writes the response.
questions.onCorrect: Status codes are an HTTP matter, so the handler maps the service's outcomes onto them, and the service stays free of HTTP.

misconceptions.feedback: The service applies rules and reports outcomes, but it should know nothing about HTTP. The layer that does is another one.
The repository only talks to storage.

questions.prompt: Account A holds 100 and account B holds 50. A transfer of 30 debits A and then credits B, with no transaction. The server crashes between the two statements. What is the total held by the two accounts afterwards?
hints: Debiting A leaves 70.
The credit to B never happens.
Add the two balances.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A holds 70 and B still holds 50, so the total is 120, and 30 has vanished.

questions.onCorrect: A transaction makes both statements succeed or neither, so a crash cannot lose 30.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be the total if the credit had happened too. The crash came before it.
A was debited by 30, and B was not credited.

questions.prompt: A worker sends one email per order the first time it sees a paid event for that order. The events arrive as (4, paid), (4, paid), (5, paid), (5, paid), (5, paid), (6, created), (7, paid). How many emails are sent?
hints: Only paid events send an email.
Each order is emailed once.
The orders with paid events are 4, 5 and 7.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 4, 5 and 7 each have a paid event, and order 6 does not: 3 emails.

questions.onCorrect: The worker sends at most one email per order, however many times the event is delivered.

misconceptions.feedback: Repeated paid events for the same order send only one email, and a created event sends none.
That counts every event. Duplicates and created events do not send email.

questions.prompt: The events are (1, paid), (1, paid), (2, paid), (3, created) and (2, paid). After the first three events have been handled, how many emails have been sent?
hints: The first event sends an email for order 1.
The second repeats order 1.
The third is a new order.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Order 1 on the first event and order 2 on the third: 2.

questions.onCorrect: Each new order with a paid event sends one email, and a repeat sends none.

misconceptions.feedback: The second event is a repeat for order 1, and it sends nothing.
The third event is a paid event for a new order, so it sends one.

questions.prompt: The events are (20, paid), (21, paid), (20, paid), (22, created) and (21, paid), and the worker sends one email per order on its first paid event. How many emails are sent in all?
hints: Order 20 is seen first, and then again.
Order 21 is also seen twice.
Order 22 only has a created event.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 20 and 21 are each emailed once, and order 22 is not: 2.

questions.onCorrect: A seen-ids set makes the second delivery of an order harmless.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every event. The repeats send nothing, and a created event sends nothing.
Order 22 has only a created event, which sends no email.

questions.prompt: A worker adds 10 to a counter for each message it handles, and remembers the ids of messages it has handled. The queue delivers m1, m2, m2 and m3, starting from a counter of 0. What does the counter hold?
hints: The second m2 is a duplicate.
Only three distinct messages arrived.
Each distinct message adds 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: m1, m2 and m3 each add 10: 30.

questions.onCorrect: Without the memory of ids the duplicate would add 10 again, and the counter would show 40.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the duplicate m2 as well. A worker that tracks ids skips it.
Each distinct message adds 10, and there are three of them.

questions.prompt: Which kind of check returns 503 until the service's database connection works?
hints: It says whether the service is ready for traffic.
It is different from the check that says the process is up.
questions.onCorrect: A health check says the process is running, and a readiness check also confirms what it depends on, such as the database.

misconceptions.feedback: A health check says the process is up. The check that also covers the database is a different one.

questions.prompt: A worker sends one email per order the first time it sees a paid event for that order. The events are (10, paid), (11, created), (10, paid), (12, paid), (12, paid) and (11, paid). How many emails are sent?
hints: List the orders that have a paid event.
Count each order once.
Order 11 has a created event and then a paid event.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 10, 11 and 12 are each emailed once: 3.

questions.onCorrect: Orders 10, 11 and 12 each have a paid event, so each gets one email, however often it repeats.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every event. A repeat for an order already emailed sends nothing.
Only paid events send email, and they belong to three different orders.

questions.prompt: What delivery guarantee does a queue give when it retries a message until it is acknowledged?
hints: The message may arrive more than once.
It never loses a message, but it may repeat one.
questions.onCorrect: Retrying until acknowledged means a message can be delivered twice, so consumers have to tolerate duplicates.

misconceptions.feedback: Exactly-once is not what a retrying queue gives. A message that is retried can arrive twice.
At-most-once would risk losing messages. A queue that retries until acknowledged can deliver one more than once.

questions.prompt: Why is it a poor design to send a confirmation email inside the database transaction of the request?
hints: Think about what happens if the transaction is rolled back after the email left.
Think about what a slow mail server does to a transaction.

acceptedIdeas: A slow mail server holds the transaction open, and a rollback cannot unsend the email
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A slow mail server holds the transaction open, and a rollback cannot unsend the email

questions.onCorrect: The email belongs after the commit, put on a queue, so that a slow server cannot hold locks and a rollback cannot leave a mistaken message.

misconceptions.feedback: A transaction can hold many statements, and that is its purpose.
A transaction does not multiply an email. The trouble lies in when the email is sent in relation to the commit.
The client does not send the confirmation. The server or a worker does.

choices.label: A transaction can hold only one statement, so the email would need its own
The email would be sent once for each statement in the transaction
Email must always be sent by the client, never by the server or a worker
A slow mail server holds the transaction open, and a rollback cannot unsend the email

questions.prompt: The request line is `GET /items?tag=red&tag=large&sort=price HTTP/1.1`. Which list gives the `name=value` pairs in its query?
hints: The query is everything after the question mark, and an ampersand separates one pair from the next.
Ask whether a name that appears twice is joined into one pair or kept as two.
questions.onCorrect: A name may repeat, as tag does here, and each repetition is its own pair. That is how a client sends several values for one parameter.

misconceptions.feedback: The query is not merged: each occurrence of tag is written out as its own pair, and the server decides what to do with the two values.
The path /items and the question mark come before the query. The query is only what follows the question mark.
The second `tag=large` is a pair too. A repeated name does not cancel the first one, so the query holds three pairs.

choices.label: `tag=red` and `sort=price`
`/items?tag=red`, `tag=large` and `sort=price`
`tag=red` and `tag=large` and `sort=price`
`tag=red,large` and `sort=price`

questions.prompt: A shop's admin page has GET links of the form /items/9/remove that delete an item, and a search crawler follows every link on the page. What happens?
hints: A crawler assumes that a GET changes nothing.
Each link names a different item, and following it sends the request that removes that item.
questions.onCorrect: Crawlers, caches and prefetching browsers all assume that a GET is read-only, so a GET that deletes data gets triggered by software nobody was watching.

acceptedIdeas: The crawler deletes the item behind every link it follows
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The crawler deletes the item behind every link it follows

misconceptions.feedback: A crawler reads a page by sending a GET request for each link, and the server carries out whatever that request does, so a link that deletes an item deletes it when the crawler follows the link.
Idempotence covers repeats of the same request. These links name different items, so each one is a different request and each removes its own item.
HTTP only defines GET as read-only. Nothing stops a server from deleting on a GET, and a server that does so will carry out the deletions for any client that asks.

choices.label: Nothing is deleted, because a crawler only reads pages
The crawler deletes the item behind every link it follows
The server refuses the requests, because a GET may not change data
Only the first item is deleted, because GET is idempotent

questions.prompt: A response with `Cache-Control: max-age=120` was stored by a cache at t = 0 seconds. A request for the same resource arrives at t = 95 seconds. What does the cache do?
hints: `max-age=120` allows the copy to be reused for 120 seconds after it was generated.
Compare the 95 seconds that have passed with the 120 seconds allowed.
questions.onCorrect: The copy is 95 seconds old and its lifetime is 120, so it is still fresh for another 25 seconds and the origin is not contacted.

acceptedIdeas: It answers from the stored copy without contacting the origin
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It answers from the stored copy without contacting the origin

misconceptions.feedback: A cache checks only when a copy is stale. This one is 95 seconds old and its lifetime is 120 seconds, so it is fresh and can be reused without any contact.
Freshness has no margin: a copy is fresh for as long as its age is below its lifetime. At 95 seconds the copy has 25 seconds left, so no check is needed yet.

choices.label: It sends the request to the origin, because 95 seconds is close to 120
It answers from the stored copy without contacting the origin
It sends the request to the origin, because a cache must check every request

questions.prompt: A router matches the path `/customers/17/orders/42/items/7` against the template `/customers/{cid}/orders/{oid}/items/{iid}`. Which values does it capture?
hints: Only the segments in braces capture a value; the others must simply be equal.
Each braces segment takes the path segment in the same position.
questions.onCorrect: Each braces segment captures the path segment in the same position, so the router returns `cid = 17`, `oid = 42` and `iid = 7` and hands them to the code for that template.

misconceptions.feedback: Those words are the fixed segments, which have to be equal in the path and the template and capture nothing. Only the segments in braces capture, and they capture the values between the fixed words.
The template has a third segment in braces, `{iid}`, and it captures 7. A path fits only when every segment of the template is matched, so none is left over.
Captures follow position from left to right. The first segment in braces takes the first value in the same place in the path, which is 17.

choices.label: `cid = customers`, `oid = orders`, `iid = items`
`cid = 17` and `oid = 42`, with the last segment left unmatched

questions.prompt: A program passes the text `{"a":1,}` to a JSON parser. What does the parser do?
hints: Ask whether the grammar has any room for a comma that separates nothing from nothing.
A parser works on the text as a whole, and it has to give one answer for it.
questions.onCorrect: JSON allows a comma only between two members, so the trailing comma makes the whole text invalid and no part of it is used.

acceptedIdeas: It rejects the whole text as invalid
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rejects the whole text as invalid

misconceptions.feedback: Some programming languages tolerate a trailing comma, but the JSON grammar does not. The comma separates two members, and here there is no second member.
A JSON parser has no partial credit: the text is either valid or it is not, and an invalid text yields no object at all, not even the part before the fault.

choices.label: It accepts the text and ignores the extra comma
It rejects the whole text as invalid
It reads `a = 1` and discards the rest of the text

questions.prompt: A profile holds `nick` `"ann"`, `bio` `"hi"` and `city` `"Rome"`. A `PATCH` sends `{"nick": null, "bio": ""}`. What does the profile hold afterwards?
hints: Null, an empty string and a field left out are three different instructions.
A field that is left out of a PATCH body is not mentioned, so it is left as it was.
questions.onCorrect: Null clears the nickname, the empty string is a value of its own, and city was not mentioned, so it keeps its old value.

misconceptions.feedback: An empty string is not `null`. `{"bio": ""}` sets the bio to a string with no characters, which is a value, whereas `null` would clear it.
A null in a PATCH clears the field it names, so the nickname is cleared rather than left as it was.
A field that is left out of the body is not mentioned, so city keeps the value it had. Only fields named in the body change.

choices.label: nick null, bio "", city null
nick null, bio null, city "Rome"
nick "ann", bio "", city "Rome"
nick null, bio "", city "Rome"

questions.prompt: The Order schema requires item (string) and qty (integer), and note (string) is optional. Properties the schema does not list are allowed. Which of these bodies does a validator reject?
hints: Check each required property for presence, and then each property that is present for its declared type.
A property that the schema does not list is not an error.
questions.onCorrect: The qty is the string "two", where the schema declares an integer, so the validator reports a type error even though both required properties are present.

misconceptions.feedback: Both required properties are present with the right types, and a property the schema does not list is allowed, so this body passes.
The optional note is a string, as declared, and both required properties are present and correctly typed, so this body passes.
The order in which properties appear does not matter. Both required properties are present with the right types, so this body passes.

choices.label: `{"item":"pen","qty":3,"colour":"red"}`
`{"item":"pen","qty":3,"note":"gift"}`
`{"qty":2,"item":"ink"}`
`{"item":"ink","qty":"two"}`

questions.prompt: The `Order` schema requires `item` (string) and `qty` (integer). A validator reports every fault it finds in the body `{"qty":"3"}`. What does it report?
hints: Check each required property for presence first.
Then check each property that is present for its declared type.
questions.onCorrect: The body has two separate faults, a missing required property and a value of the wrong type, and a validator reports each of them so that the client can fix both at once.

acceptedIdeas: Both: `item` is missing and `qty` has the wrong type
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both: `item` is missing and `qty` has the wrong type

misconceptions.feedback: The missing item is one fault, but the qty is the string "3" where an integer is declared, which is a second fault. A validator reports each fault it finds.
The wrong type of qty is one fault, but item is required and absent, which is a second fault. A validator reports each fault it finds.
Properties listed under required must be present. The optional ones may be left out, and item is not optional.

choices.label: Only that `item` is missing
Only that `qty` has the wrong type
Nothing, because a body may leave out properties
Both: `item` is missing and `qty` has the wrong type

questions.prompt: Ids 50 down to 41 are listed newest first. A client fetches page 1 with `limit=4` and `offset=0` and receives 50, 49, 48 and 47. Then ids 51, 52 and 53 are added at the top, and the client fetches page 2 with `limit=4` and `offset=4`. What does page 2 contain?
hints: Write the new list from 53 downwards, and count four places from the top to find where page 2 begins.
Compare what page 2 contains with 50, 49, 48 and 47.
questions.onCorrect: The three new rows push everything down three places, so page 2 is 49, 48, 47 and 46, and three of its four rows were already on page 1.

acceptedIdeas: Mostly rows the client has already seen on page 1
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mostly rows the client has already seen on page 1

misconceptions.feedback: An offset counts from the top of the list as it is now, and the three new rows have moved everything down. Four places from the top is no longer the row after 47.
The new rows are at the top of the list, in places 0 to 2, and an offset of 4 skips past them. Page 2 begins at the fifth row from the top.

choices.label: Mainly the three new rows, followed by one old row
Rows 46, 45, 44 and 43, which continue where page 1 stopped
Mostly rows the client has already seen on page 1

questions.prompt: A balance is 100. A client sends `POST /charges` for 30 and, after two timeouts, sends the same request twice more, so the server receives it three times. The server does nothing to recognise repeats. What is the balance afterwards?
hints: Ask what the server has to go on when the third copy arrives.
A plain POST carries nothing that says it is a repeat.
questions.onCorrect: With no way to recognise a repeat, the server carries out each copy as a new charge, so 100 - 30 - 30 - 30 leaves 10.

acceptedIdeas: 10, because the server carries out all three copies
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 10, because the server carries out all three copies

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in a plain POST tells the server that it has seen the request before, so each copy is carried out as a new charge. Charging once is what an idempotency key makes possible.
A server keeps no memory of requests it has seen unless it is built to. Without a key or a similar record it treats every copy as new and carries it out.

choices.label: 70, because the server charges once however many copies arrive
10, because the server carries out all three copies
100, because the server rejects a request it has already seen

questions.prompt: Five changes are proposed. (a) add an optional response field `nick`. (b) remove the response field `name`. (c) change `id` from integer to string. (d) add the endpoint `/orders/{id}/notes`. (e) make the request field `currency` required, though it was optional. Which of these lists contains every breaking change?
hints: Ask for each change whether a client written against the old contract could fail.
Removing, retyping and newly requiring are the three kinds to look for, and additions do not break old clients.
questions.onCorrect: Removing a field, changing its type and making a request field required each make a client written against the old contract fail, whereas the new optional field and the new endpoint are additions.

acceptedIdeas: Removing name, changing the type of id and requiring currency
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Removing name, changing the type of id and requiring currency

misconceptions.feedback: Changing id from an integer to a string also breaks a client that reads it as an integer, and requiring currency breaks every caller that used to leave it out.
Making currency required breaks callers that used to leave it out, so it belongs with the breaking changes.
The new optional field nick and the new endpoint are additions. A client ignores what it has never heard of, so neither breaks anything.

choices.label: Removing name and changing the type of id
All five, because every change alters the contract
Only removing name
Removing name, changing the type of id and requiring currency

questions.prompt: Five client apps use an API. Three read the field qty, and two read only id and name. The server removes qty and adds quantity in the same version. Which clients fail?
hints: Ask which clients depend on the field that has gone.
A client that never reads a field does not notice that it has changed.
questions.onCorrect: A client fails when it relies on something that is gone, and only the three that read qty rely on it. The new field quantity does not help them, because they were never written to look for it.

misconceptions.feedback: The two clients that read only id and name do not depend on qty, so they keep working.
A client ignores a field it has never heard of, so the addition of quantity breaks nothing. The removal of qty is what causes failures.
The three old clients look for qty by name, and the same value under a new name does not help them. They find nothing where they expect it.

choices.label: None, because quantity carries the same value as qty
All five, because the contract changed
The two that read only id and name, because a new field appeared
The three that read qty

questions.prompt: An old response has six fields: id, name, qty, price, note and status. The new one drops note, renames status to state, changes price from an integer to a string, and adds a field tags. Which old fields fail the compatibility check?
hints: An old field fails if it is missing or if its type has changed.
A renamed field is missing under its old name, and a field that was added is not an old field.
questions.onCorrect: Each old field is checked for presence and type: note and status are missing and price has changed type, while id, name and qty are untouched and adding tags breaks nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: Changing price from an integer to a string also fails the check, because a client that reads it as a number can no longer do so.
A field that is dropped or renamed is missing under its old name, and a client that reads it finds nothing, so note and status fail as well.
The field tags is an addition. The check is made on the old fields, and an extra field in the new response fails nothing.

choices.label: note, status and price
note, status, price and tags
price only
note and status only

questions.prompt: The `users` table has 3 rows. A handler builds `SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '<input>'` by joining strings, and receives the input `x' OR '1'='1`. How many rows come back?
hints: Write out the query after the input has been joined into it, and read the condition as the database will.
The quotation mark in the input closes the string that was meant to hold a name.
questions.onCorrect: The joined query reads `name = 'x' OR '1'='1'`, and the second condition is true for every row, so all three rows come back.

misconceptions.feedback: No rows would come back if the input were compared as a name, because nobody has that name. Joined into the query, though, it becomes part of the condition, and `OR '1'='1'` is true for every row.
Nothing in the joined query picks out a single user. The added condition is true for every row, so every row matches.

choices.label: All three rows
One row
No rows

questions.prompt: A handler runs `SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?` and sends the value `x' OR '1'='1` separately as a parameter. What does the database do with that value?
hints: Ask whether the database ever reads the value as part of the query.
The value is sent separately from the query text.
questions.onCorrect: The value is compared as an ordinary string, so the query looks for a user with exactly that name, and none exists.

acceptedIdeas: It compares the value as an ordinary name, so no row matches
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It compares the value as an ordinary name, so no row matches

misconceptions.feedback: That happens when the input is joined into the query text. A parameter is sent separately, so the database never treats any part of it as query syntax.
The quotation mark is only a character in the value. The database does not parse the value as part of the query, so nothing about it is malformed.

choices.label: It compares the value as an ordinary name, so no row matches
It reads the OR as part of the query, so every row matches
It rejects the query as malformed because of the quotation mark

questions.prompt: Invoices 17, 18, 19 and 20 belong to users 4, 9, 4 and 9 in that order. User 9 requests all four, and the handler checks the owner on each request. Which invoices are returned?
hints: The check compares each invoice's owner with the caller, user 9.
A request for an invoice that fails the check is refused.
questions.onCorrect: The check passes only where the owner is the caller, which is invoices 18 and 20. The requests for 17 and 19 are refused.

misconceptions.feedback: Being logged in only says who is asking. The check compares each invoice's owner with the caller, and user 4 owns 17 and 19.
Those belong to user 4. The check lets a caller through only for invoices that the caller owns, and the caller here is user 9.
Each request is checked on its own, so a request that fails the check does not stop the others from passing it.

choices.label: Invoices 18 and 20
None, because the first request already failed the check
All four, because user 9 is logged in
Invoices 17 and 19

questions.prompt: A bucket holds at most 3 tokens, refills at 1 token a second and starts full. Each allowed request spends one token. Four requests arrive at the same instant. What happens?
hints: Ask how many tokens the bucket holds when the first request arrives.
No time passes between the four requests, so nothing is added to the bucket.
questions.onCorrect: The full bucket holds 3 tokens and no time passes, so the first three requests spend them and the fourth finds the bucket empty.

acceptedIdeas: Three are allowed and the fourth is refused
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Three are allowed and the fourth is refused

misconceptions.feedback: The refill adds tokens only as time passes, at 1 a second. Four requests at the same instant leave no time for any to be added.
The refill rate sets the long-run pace. A bucket that starts full has 3 tokens to spend at once, so a burst of up to its capacity gets through.

choices.label: Three are allowed and the fourth is refused
Only one is allowed, because the refill rate is 1 token a second
All four are allowed, because the bucket refills as the requests arrive

questions.prompt: A client sent six idempotent requests and got these results: 200, 400, 429, 503, 404 and a timeout. Which of them are worth retrying after a wait?
hints: A request that succeeded needs no retry, and a request that is wrong will fail the same way again.
The failures that may clear with time are a timeout, a 429 and a 503.
questions.onCorrect: The 429, the 503 and the timeout may succeed later. The 200 needs no retry, and the 400 and the 404 will fail again until the request itself changes.

misconceptions.feedback: A timeout is also worth retrying, because the request may simply have been lost and a later attempt can succeed. For an idempotent request a repeat is safe.
A 400 and a 404 fail in the same way every time until the request is changed, so retrying them only adds load. The 429 and the 503 clear with time.
A 400 means the request was malformed and a 404 means nothing exists at that address. Neither will change by waiting, so retrying them only adds load.

choices.label: 429, 503 and the timeout
429 and 503 only
400, 404 and the timeout
Every result except the 200

questions.prompt: A worker sends one email per order, the first time it sees a paid event for that order. The events arrive as (4, paid), (4, paid), (5, paid), (5, paid), (5, paid), (6, created) and (7, paid). Which orders are emailed?
hints: A created event is not a paid event, so it sends no email.
The worker remembers the orders it has already handled, and skips a repeat.
questions.onCorrect: Orders 4, 5 and 7 each have a paid event, and the worker emails each one only on its first. The repeats are skipped, and the created event for order 6 sends nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: A queue that retries delivers some messages more than once, and a worker that emailed on every delivery would send duplicates. This worker remembers the orders it has handled and skips a repeat.
Order 6 has only a created event, and the worker sends an email on a paid event. A created event sends nothing.
Order 5 has paid events too, and the worker emails it on the first of them. Several deliveries of one event still count as one email, not none.

choices.label: Orders 4, 4, 5, 5, 5 and 7, once for every paid event
Orders 4, 5 and 7
Orders 4 and 7
Orders 4, 5, 6 and 7

questions.prompt: A shop has 5 orders, numbered 1 to 5. The request `DELETE /orders/4` is delivered three times. Which orders does the shop hold afterwards?
hints: Order 4 can be removed only once.
Ask what the second and third deliveries find when they look for order 4.
questions.onCorrect: The state after three deliveries is the state after one. Only the response differs, a 404 for the later ones, because order 4 is no longer there to remove.

acceptedIdeas: Orders 1, 2, 3 and 5, the same as after one delivery
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Orders 1, 2, 3 and 5, the same as after one delivery

misconceptions.feedback: Each delivery names order 4, and only the first finds it. The later ones have nothing to remove, so they cannot take any other order away.
A DELETE only removes. Nothing in the later deliveries puts order 4 back, so it stays gone.

choices.label: All five orders, because the later deliveries restore what the first removed
Orders 1, 2, 3 and 5, the same as after one delivery
Only two orders, because each of the three deliveries removes one

questions.prompt: The Order schema requires item (string) and qty (integer), and note (string) is optional. Which of these bodies does a validator accept?
hints: Check each required property for presence, and then each property that is present for its declared type.
A string with no characters is still a string, and zero is still an integer.
questions.onCorrect: Both required properties are present, and an empty string is still a string and 0 is still an integer, so the body matches the schema.

misconceptions.feedback: The number 2.5 is not an integer, so qty fails its declared type.
The number 7 is not a string, so item fails its declared type.
The property qty is listed under required, so a body without it is invalid.

choices.label: `{"item":"cup"}`

questions.prompt: A worker sends one email per order the first time it sees a paid event for that order. The events arrive as (10, paid), (11, created), (10, paid), (12, paid), (12, paid) and (11, paid). Which orders are emailed, and in what order?
hints: A created event sends no email, and it does not use up the order's one email.
Go through the events in order, and note each order at its first paid event.
questions.onCorrect: Order 10 is emailed at its first paid event, order 12 at its first, and order 11 only at its paid event, which comes last, since its created event sent nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: Order 11 first appears in a created event, which sends no email. Its paid event comes after the first paid event for order 12, so it is emailed last.
Order 11 has a paid event at the end of the stream, and nothing has been sent for it before then, so that event sends its email.
A worker that emailed on every delivery would send duplicates. This one remembers the orders it has handled and skips a repeat.

choices.label: Orders 10, 12 and 11, in that order
Orders 10 and 12 only, because order 11 was only created
Orders 10, 11 and 12, in that order
Orders 10, 10, 12, 12 and 11, once for every paid event

questions.prompt: Which of these groups of changes contains only breaking changes?
hints: A change is breaking if a client written against the old contract can fail because of it.
Additions, such as a new endpoint or an optional field, do not break old clients.
questions.onCorrect: Renaming a field, newly requiring a request field and changing a type each make an old client fail, whereas the additions in the other groups do not.

acceptedIdeas: Renaming a response field, making an optional request field required and changing a field from integer to string
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Renaming a response field, making an optional request field required and changing a field from integer to string

misconceptions.feedback: All three are additions, and a client ignores what it has never heard of, so none of them breaks an old client.
The rename breaks clients that read the old name, but the endpoint and the optional field are additions that break nothing.
Making a field required and lowering a length limit break callers that used to succeed, but a new optional query parameter breaks nobody.

choices.label: Adding an optional query parameter, making an optional request field required and lowering a length limit
Adding an endpoint, adding an optional response field and adding an optional query parameter
Renaming a response field, adding an endpoint and adding an optional response field
Renaming a response field, making an optional request field required and changing a field from integer to string

questions.prompt: The ü takes two bytes, but only one byte is added to the count of 17. Why?
hints: Ask what the count of 17 already includes for the ü.

acceptedIdeas: The ü is already counted once among the 17 characters, so only its second byte is new
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ü is already counted once among the 17 characters, so only its second byte is new

questions.onCorrect: Each character is counted once in the 17, so a character of two bytes adds one byte beyond that.

choices.label: A character can only ever add one extra byte, however it is encoded
The ü is already counted once among the 17 characters, so only its second byte is new
`Content-Length` leaves out the second byte of every two-byte character

misconceptions.feedback: UTF-8 gives some characters three or four bytes, so the extra amount depends on the character and not on a fixed rule of one.
`Content-Length` counts every byte of the body, so no byte of the ü is left out.

questions.prompt: The resend arrives when the counter already holds 15. Why does the counter still hold 15 afterwards?
hints: Compare what a PUT asks for with what a POST asks for.

acceptedIdeas: A `PUT` states the counter's value, so repeating it changes nothing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A `PUT` states the counter's value, so repeating it changes nothing

questions.onCorrect: A PUT states the value the counter should end with, so a second delivery sets what is already there.

choices.label: The server recognises the resend and ignores it
A `PUT` can only be carried out once for each address
A `PUT` states the counter's value, so repeating it changes nothing

misconceptions.feedback: The server has no way to recognise a repeated request unless it is built to. The outcome comes from what the PUT asks for.
A PUT can be sent as often as the client likes. Nothing limits it to one delivery.

questions.prompt: The counter holds 10. The request `PUT /counter` with the body `{"value": 15}` is delivered twice. By how much does the second delivery change the counter?
hints: PUT says what the counter should be, not how much to add.
Work out what the first delivery leaves in the counter.
Compare the value the second delivery sets with the value already there.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first delivery sets the counter to 15. The second sets it to 15 again, so it changes nothing.

questions.onCorrect: PUT states the end value, so the second delivery sets what is already there and changes nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how much the first delivery changed the counter. The second one finds the counter already at 15.
15 is the value the counter holds. The question asks how much the second delivery changes it.

questions.prompt: A shop's page has a link `GET /cart/clear` that empties the shopper's cart, and the shopper's browser prefetches the links on a page to make them open faster. What happens?
hints: Browsers prefetch links, and they assume that a GET changes nothing.
Ask who decided to send the request.

acceptedIdeas: The cart is emptied before the shopper clicks anything
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cart is emptied before the shopper clicks anything

questions.onCorrect: Browsers, caches and crawlers all assume that a GET is read-only, so a GET that empties a cart is triggered by software nobody was watching.

choices.label: Nothing is emptied, because prefetching only reads pages
The browser refuses to prefetch it, because a GET may not change data
The cart is emptied once, because GET is idempotent
The cart is emptied before the shopper clicks anything

misconceptions.feedback: The server carries out whatever a request asks, so a link that empties the cart empties it when the browser fetches the link.
HTTP only defines GET as read-only. Nothing stops a server from changing data on a GET, and nothing stops a browser from sending it.
Idempotence is about what repeats do. It does not stop the first fetch from carrying out the request.

questions.prompt: A valid, permitted request reaches a server whose database is down for maintenance, and the server knows it will be back in ten minutes. Which status code fits best?
hints: The fault is the server's, so the class begins with 5.
Ask whether the server failed unexpectedly or knows that it cannot serve for now.
questions.onCorrect: 503 says the server cannot serve right now, so the client can try again later, whereas a 500 reports a failure nobody expected.

choices.label: 503 Service Unavailable
500 Internal Server Error
400 Bad Request

misconceptions.feedback: A 500 reports an unexpected failure. Here the server knows why it cannot answer, and the condition is temporary, so a more specific code in the same class exists.
400 blames the client's request, and this request was fine. The fault lies with the server.

questions.prompt: A cache holds a copy whose Last-Modified date is 3 November 2026, and it revalidates by sending If-Modified-Since with that date. The resource was changed on 5 November 2026. Which status code does the origin reply with?
hints: If-Modified-Since asks whether the resource changed after that date.
Compare the date the cache holds with the date of the change.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The resource changed after the date the cache holds, so the origin sends the new version with 200 OK and not 304.

questions.onCorrect: The change is newer than the date in the request, so the origin answers with the new body and the cache replaces its copy.

misconceptions.feedback: A 304 says the copy is still current. The resource changed after the date the cache sent, so the copy is out of date.
412 reports that a precondition failed, as for a conditional write. For a read that finds a change, a different code is used.

questions.prompt: Why must the cache contact the origin at t = 350?
hints: Age is measured from the moment the copy was fetched.
Compare the age with the lifetime of 300 seconds.

acceptedIdeas: The copy's age is 350 seconds, which is above its lifetime of 300
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The copy's age is 350 seconds, which is above its lifetime of 300

questions.onCorrect: The copy was fetched at t = 0, so at t = 350 it is 350 seconds old, which is more than 300 and makes it stale.

choices.label: The copy's age is 350 seconds, which is above its lifetime of 300
Every request after t = 300 has to go to the origin
The resource has changed at the origin since t = 0

misconceptions.feedback: The cache judges a copy by its age, and not by the clock alone.
The example says the resource never changes, and a cache cannot see a change without asking.

questions.prompt: Does the path `/orders/42/items` fit the template `/orders/{id}/notes`?
hints: Compare the segments that are not in braces, one pair at a time.
The first pair is equal. Look at the last pair.
questions.onCorrect: The counts agree and the first segment matches, but the last fixed segments differ, so the path does not fit and the router moves on to the next template.

choices.label: Yes, because the counts agree and `{id}` captures 42
No, because the path has more segments than the template
No, because `items` does not equal `notes`

misconceptions.feedback: A path fits only when every segment that is not in braces is equal, and the counts agreeing is not enough.
Both have three segments, as the first line of the example shows.

questions.prompt: An order has 3 units at a price of 4.35 and 2 units at a price of 1.10. What is the total in integer cents?
hints: Convert each price to whole cents first.
4.35 is 435 cents and 1.10 is 110 cents.
Multiply each price by its number of units, then add the two lines.
questions.onCorrect: Each line is converted to whole cents and multiplied, and the sum of whole numbers is exact.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total in dollars. The question asks for cents.
That adds the two prices in cents. Each price is multiplied by its own number of units first.

questions.prompt: Why does the operation list a 400 response as well as a 201?
hints: Ask what a client written from this document would do when a request has an invalid body.

acceptedIdeas: A client has to handle failures as well as success, so the contract states both
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A client has to handle failures as well as success, so the contract states both

questions.onCorrect: The operation documents 201 and 400, so a client can handle both without reading the server's code.

choices.label: A client has to handle failures as well as success, so the contract states both
A 400 response is required whenever an operation has a request body
A 201 response cannot be documented without a second response beside it

misconceptions.feedback: OpenAPI does not demand any particular error response. Listing it is a choice that comes from what clients need.
Each response is documented on its own. A 201 can stand alone as the description of success.

questions.prompt: The `Order` schema requires `item` (a string) and `qty` (an integer). How many errors does a validator report for the body `{"item":5,"qty":2.5}`?
hints: Check each required property for presence first.
Then check the type of each value against the schema.
2.5 is a number, but it is not a whole number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both required properties are present. item is the number 5, where a string is declared, and qty is 2.5, which is not an integer: 2 errors.

questions.onCorrect: Each present property is checked against its declared type, and both values fail, so the validator reports two errors.

misconceptions.feedback: Both properties are present, but presence is not the only check. Look at the type of each value.
Check both values against their declared types, and not only one of them.

questions.prompt: A list of products is sorted by price, cheapest first, and several products cost 4.99. The last product a client saw costs 4.99 and has id 12. What should the cursor hold so that the next page starts in exactly the right place?
hints: The cursor has to name one exact place in the sorted order.
Ask what two products with the same price have that tells them apart.
questions.onCorrect: The price gives the place in the order, and the unique id settles the products that tie on it, so the pair names one exact row.

choices.label: The price, 4.99
The id, 12
The price and the id

misconceptions.feedback: Several products share the price 4.99, so the price alone does not name one place in the order, and rows can be skipped or repeated.
The list is sorted by price and not by id, so the id alone does not say where in the order the last product sits.

questions.prompt: A handler is writing the error body for a failed charge. Which member should it not send to the caller?
hints: Think about what would help an attacker.
Which of these shows how the server works inside?
questions.onCorrect: A file name, a line number and a SQL statement show how the server is built, so they belong in its own logs and not in a response.

choices.label: `"title": "The card was declined"`
`"detail": "charges.py line 88: SELECT * FROM cards"`
`"detail": "The expiry date is in the past."`
`"type": "https://api.shop.example/problems/card-declined"`

misconceptions.feedback: A short title is for a person to read. This one describes the problem and shows nothing about the server.
A detail may say what the client can fix. An expired date is exactly that, and it shows nothing about the server.
A type is a stable name for the kind of error. It is an identifier and not a view into the server.

questions.prompt: Why does the response keep `qty` while `quantity` is added?
hints: Ask who still reads the old name during the migration.

acceptedIdeas: Old clients still read `qty`, and would fail if it vanished at once
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Old clients still read `qty`, and would fail if it vanished at once

questions.onCorrect: Serving both lets old clients keep reading `qty` while new clients move to `quantity`.

choices.label: Old clients still read `qty`, and would fail if it vanished at once
New clients need both fields to work out the quantity
A response must keep every field name it has ever used

misconceptions.feedback: New clients read `quantity` and ignore `qty`. They do not need the old name.
A field can be removed once no client reads it. Nothing requires old names to stay for ever.

questions.prompt: The handler has loaded invoice 18 for caller 9. What must it compare with the caller's id before it returns the invoice?
hints: The handler already has the caller's id from the token. It needs something from the invoice to compare it with.

acceptedIdeas: The id of the user who owns the invoice
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The id of the user who owns the invoice

questions.onCorrect: The handler loads the object and compares its owner with the authenticated caller.

choices.label: The id of the invoice, 18
The caller's own id from the token, 9
The id of the user who owns the invoice

misconceptions.feedback: That is the invoice's own id. It names the invoice and says nothing about who may have it.
Comparing the caller with their own id would always match, and it would prove nothing.

questions.prompt: `DELETE /documents/{id}` deletes a document whenever the caller is logged in. Which fix addresses the flaw?
hints: The flaw is that any logged-in caller can delete any document.
Which change refuses a caller who does not own it?

acceptedIdeas: Check that the caller owns the document
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Check that the caller owns the document

questions.onCorrect: The server has to compare the owner of the object with the caller on every request.

choices.label: Use longer, random document ids
Check that the caller owns the document
Hide the delete button in the page
Require HTTPS on every request

misconceptions.feedback: Longer ids make guessing harder, but a caller who learns an id can still use it.
A hidden button does not stop a request. The server enforces the rule, and the page does not.
HTTPS protects the data in transit. It does not decide whose document it is.

questions.prompt: A handler runs `SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?` and sends the value `'; DROP TABLE users; --` separately as a parameter. What does the database do with that value?
hints: Ask whether the database ever reads the value as part of the query.
The value is sent separately from the query text.

acceptedIdeas: It compares the value as an ordinary name, so no row matches
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It compares the value as an ordinary name, so no row matches

questions.onCorrect: The value is compared as an ordinary string, so the query looks for a user with exactly that name, and none exists.

choices.label: It runs the `DROP TABLE` statement before the comparison
It rejects the query as malformed because of the semicolon
It compares the value as an ordinary name, so no row matches

misconceptions.feedback: That happens when the value is joined into the query text. A parameter is sent separately, so the database never treats any part of it as query syntax.
The semicolon is only a character in the value. The database does not parse the value as part of the query, so nothing about it is malformed.

questions.prompt: A client retries six times. The first wait is 300 ms, and each wait doubles the one before it, but no wait is longer than 4000 ms. What is the total waiting time in milliseconds?
hints: Write out the waits one by one, doubling each time.
A wait that would pass 4000 is held at 4000.
Add the six waits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The waits are 300, 600, 1200, 2400, 4000 and 4000 ms, because doubling would give 4800 and 9600 for the last two and the cap holds each at 4000. They add up to 12500 ms.

questions.onCorrect: The cap limits the fifth and sixth waits to 4000 ms, so the total is smaller than with doubling alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 4800 and 9600 for the last two waits. The cap holds each at 4000.
That is the total of the first five waits. The sixth adds another 4000.
That adds only the four waits that stay below the cap. There are two more.

questions.prompt: The events are (20, paid), (21, paid), (20, paid), (22, created) and (22, paid), and the worker sends one email per order on its first paid event. How many emails are sent in all?
hints: Order 20 is seen first, and then again.
A created event sends nothing, and it does not use up an order's one email.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 20 and 21 are each emailed at their first paid event, and order 22 is emailed at its paid event, which is its first. The repeat of order 20 and the created event send nothing: 3 emails.

questions.onCorrect: Orders 20, 21 and 22 each reach a first paid event, so three emails go out, and the repeat of order 20 sends none.

misconceptions.feedback: Order 22 has a paid event as well as a created one, and the paid event is its first, so it sends an email.
That counts every event. A repeat sends nothing, and a created event sends nothing.
That also counts the created event for order 22. A created event sends no email.

questions.prompt: The service is running, but its database is down for two minutes. Restarting the service would not help, and it should not receive traffic until the database is back. Which check should report the failure?
hints: One check decides whether the process is restarted, and the other decides whether it is sent traffic.
questions.onCorrect: A readiness check also confirms what the service depends on, so it fails while the database is down and the service stays out of rotation without being restarted.

choices.label: The health check
Both checks
The readiness check
